categories.description_en: Tasks a professional is paid for: legal analysis, finance and tax questions, office documents, spreadsheets, research memos and other desk work. The tests here hand the model a realistic brief and judge the finished product, often with a human expert or an expert-written rubric.

Changing and repairing real programs. The model works inside a repository or a terminal over many steps, reads the code, runs commands, and is scored on whether the resulting change passes hidden tests or a reviewer. This is the busiest category on every launch page.

Training and improving models rather than ordinary software: reproducing a research paper, running an experiment, tuning a training recipe, writing a compute kernel. The score is usually whether the resulting artifact works or reaches a target.

Mathematics from contest problems to research-level questions, plus scientific reasoning and laboratory knowledge in chemistry, physics and biology. Dangerous biological capabilities are kept out of this category and sit under Biosecurity.

Finding, matching and using information spread across very long inputs: hundreds of thousands or a million tokens of documents, transcripts or structured data. The tests plant facts or relationships deep in the input and check whether the model can still use them.

Operating a computer the way a person does: a desktop, a browser, a mobile device, through screenshots and clicks rather than an API. Tasks are everyday chores in real applications, scored on whether the end state is correct. Open-ended web research has its own category.
Images, charts, video, audio, scanned documents and sheet music, and reasoning that connects them with text. The model has to read what it sees or hears and answer about it.

Finding and fixing vulnerabilities, reproducing known flaws in controlled test environments, analysing binaries and operating production systems under failure. These tests measure capability in a sandbox; the safety category measures whether the model refuses to misuse it.

Broad knowledge, logic and abstract problem solving, factual accuracy and the mixed question sets that try to cover everything at once. The benchmarks here are the ones most often quoted as a single headline number.
Writing code from a specification without a long agentic process: a function, a component, a drawing, an algorithm. Scored by tests, by rendering the output, or by a judge comparing candidates.

Calling functions and APIs, chaining tools, planning multi-step work and carrying a long task to the end. The environments range from office automation to games, and the score is whether the whole workflow completed.
Finding hard-to-locate facts on the open web and synthesising an answer from many pages. The questions are built so that no single page answers them.
Obeying constraints: output formats, length limits, data schemas, forbidden words and multi-step user requirements. The score is how many constraints the answer honoured.
Knowledge and task performance across natural languages other than English. No publication in the catalog has printed a result here yet.
Creative and editorial writing, style, role play, and the emotional and social quality of a conversation. No publication in the catalog has printed a result here yet.
Clinical and medical knowledge, medical documents, and the quality and safety of help given in a medical conversation, usually graded against rubrics written by physicians.

Tests of dangerous biological capability and of dual-use risk: virology know-how, wet-lab troubleshooting, and whether the model refuses requests that could help build a weapon. Some sets also cover chemical and cyber risk. Here a high capability score is not good news, and the refusal scores are the ones to read.

Refusals of harmful requests, resistance to jailbreaks, honesty under pressure, sycophancy, and whether an agent discloses its own failures or takes forbidden shortcuts. Most of these are rates where lower is better; the table says so on each row.
CAD modelling, electrical engineering, spatial design and the production of engineering artifacts from a specification, scored on whether the artifact meets the spec.

Head-to-head preference rankings by people or judge models, and composite indexes that average many unrelated tests into one number. A specialised index stays in its own category; only the catch-all ones live here.

about.notes: The evaluation page gives version v1.1 but no launch date. The 'printed by Anthropic' label comes from the aggregator and was not confirmed here. Third-party mirrors (BenchLM) show scores that conflict with the Artificial Analysis page, so use the primary page for figures.
about.what_it_tests: AA-Briefcase tests AI agents on long, multi-week business projects in fields such as data science, product management and corporate strategy. The material is four multi-week projects with thousands of input files and 91 tasks in total, and each task asks for a professional deliverable such as a spreadsheet, presentation or memo. Each deliverable is graded on pass-or-fail rubric checks plus pairwise comparisons for analytical quality and presentation, and these are combined into an Elo score. The evaluation is private and run by Artificial Analysis.

about.notes: Known from the Mistral Large 4 release page (October 2026), which calls it an independent evaluation. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: The Artificial Analysis Cyber Index measures how well a model finds, reproduces and fixes security flaws in real software across several cyber tasks; the Mistral Large 4 page prints it as a count of successes, with safety blocks (refusals) shown separately.

about.notes: The Artificial Analysis announcement dated 5 August 2025 gives the 100 questions, the roughly 100,000-token document sets, the human verification and sample accuracy percentages. It gives no version number and does not define the metric or the grading method; the methodology page it points to was not opened, so the grader is unconfirmed. A search snippet mentioned a v1.1 leaderboard with newer scores, which was not verified.
about.what_it_tests: AA-LCR tests whether a model can reason across several long documents at once, rather than retrieve a single passage. The benchmark has 100 human-crafted questions, each tied to a document set averaging about 100,000 tokens (cl100k_base tokenizer), and each answer has to be inferred by combining information from several documents. Undergraduate students wrote the questions, and every question was answered correctly by at least one human tester. The published metric is accuracy, shown as a percentage on the Artificial Analysis leaderboard.

about.notes: Artificial Analysis evaluation page. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: AA-Omniscience is the Artificial Analysis knowledge and hallucination evaluation: 6,000 questions across 42 topics where a correct answer scores +1, a wrong answer -1 and an abstention 0. The Omniscience Index (-100 to 100) rewards knowing when not to answer; model cards also print the accuracy and the non-hallucination rate separately.

about.maintainer: AceBench authors (Chen Chen and co-authors, Huawei Noah's Ark Lab)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2501.12851 (January 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: AceBench tests tool use (function calling) across normal, special and agent settings: single and parallel calls, calls with imperfect instructions, and multi-turn agent dialogues where the model has to drive a simulated environment. The score is accuracy over the test cases; model cards print the English split.

about.maintainer: UC Berkeley Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (rdi-berkeley), with Snorkel AI hosting the leaderboard and contributing task work and funding. Paper: arXiv 2606.05405; code: github.com/rdi-berkeley/agents-last-exam; Snorkel lists a release date of 2026-06-09. Printed labels say Google, OpenAI and Alibaba; no source found connects those companies to the benchmark, so those attributions are unconfirmed. Aggregator pass-rate figures conflict and are not used.
about.what_it_tests: Agents' Last Exam tests AI agents on long, realistic professional tasks with checkable outcomes, covering 55 sub-industries of the non-physical economy. Agents get only a task description and work in full operating-system sandboxes, and outputs are graded against hidden, deterministic reference answers. The public release (ALE-V1) has 147 tasks drawn from a larger corpus of more than 1,500.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (13 April 2023) describes the exam sources. Model cards usually print it as exact-match accuracy with a stated number of shots.
about.what_it_tests: AGIEval tests general ability with questions taken from standardized human exams: college entrance tests, law school admission tests, math competitions and lawyer qualification exams, in English and Chinese. The score is the share of questions answered correctly.

about.maintainer: Allen Institute for AI (Aniruddha Kembhavi and co-authors)
about.notes: Paper "A Diagram Is Worth a Dozen Images" (ECCV 2016). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: AI2D is a set of about 5,000 grade-school science diagrams with multiple-choice questions about their content, such as the stages of a life cycle or the parts of a food web. Cards report accuracy on the test split; some evaluations mask the diagram labels and some do not.

about.notes: The aider leaderboard page describes the exercises and the pass rate; the benchmark was announced on 21 December 2024.
about.what_it_tests: The aider polyglot benchmark tests code editing through the aider tool on 225 Exercism exercises in C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python and Rust. The score is the share of exercises whose tests pass after the model's edits, with a second attempt allowed after seeing the test output.

about.notes: The exam has run since 1983; the benchmark use is a publisher convention and the introduced year is left empty. The year in a label (AIME 2024, AIME 2025) matters: newer exams are less likely to appear in training data. Attempt counts differ between publishers.
about.what_it_tests: The AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination) is the second round of the MAA competition series for high-school students in the United States: 15 problems in three hours, each with an integer answer from 0 to 999. As a benchmark, a given year's two exams (30 problems) are posed to a model, and the score is the share answered correctly; publishers state whether tools such as a Python interpreter were allowed.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (6 April 2024) describes the length-controlled estimator; the first AlpacaEval dates from 2023.
about.what_it_tests: AlpacaEval scores an instruction-following model by letting an LLM judge compare its answers with a baseline model's answers on a fixed prompt set. The length-controlled win rate (AlpacaEval 2.0 LC) removes the judge's preference for longer answers by predicting what the win rate would be at equal length.

about.notes: Google's methodology page was read; the 2026 date is taken from the Google blog URL path (android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/03/...), which was not opened. The family's printed label is Alibaba's AndroidBench, which the Qwen3.8 model page describes only as a 95-task public subset scored avg@3, with no description of content. Google's 2.0 set is private and has 30 tasks, and 1.0 used localized GitHub pull requests, so the printed family is not confirmed to be any Google version. Keep unverified until the Alibaba label is matched to a version record. No scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: Google's Android Bench measures how well AI models build and change Android apps. The methodology page describes version 2.0, with 30 long-horizon tasks in four streams: app creation from design mocks, migrations of production apps to newer libraries, new features, and conversions of Flutter or React Native projects. Each task runs in a fresh container with Android emulators, and the primary metric is the pass rate: every functional test passes, visual checks match and there are no constraint violations. The dataset is private.

about.maintainer: Google Research (GitHub google-research/android_world); paper first author Christopher Rawles
about.notes: The arXiv abstract page (submitted 23 May 2024, lead author Christopher Rawles, later revision shown) gives the 116 tasks, the 20 apps, the parameterized task generation and the setup, checking and teardown logic. The GitHub README (fetched) confirms the live emulator, the 116 tasks and 20 apps, and the citation, but does not explain how rewards are computed. The README also documents a MiniWoB++ variant and a step limit updated on 18 November 2024, so a card citing AndroidWorld alone does not fix the suite or step limit used.
about.what_it_tests: AndroidWorld tests whether an autonomous agent can operate Android apps on a live emulator to complete natural-language tasks. The benchmark has 116 hand-crafted tasks across 20 apps, and each task is instantiated with randomly generated parameters, which the authors describe as producing millions of task variations. Each task includes setup, success-checking and teardown logic, so runs are reproducible and rewards come from programmatic checks of app state. Publishers report the task success rate.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (submitted 20 January 2026, lead author Bertie Vidgen) gives the task count, the three professions and the Pass@1 metric; the Mercor post of 8 September 2026 describes version 1.1. A page that prints "APEX-Agents" without a version may rest on either release.
about.what_it_tests: APEX-Agents tests whether an AI agent can carry out long-horizon, cross-application professional work. The tasks were written by investment banking analysts, management consultants and corporate lawyers, and the agent completes each one inside a simulated work environment with files and tools (documents, spreadsheets, PDFs, mail, chat, calendar and a file system), with web search disabled. The result is Pass@1, the first-attempt success rate. The original release has 480 tasks; version 1.1 (September 2026) has 80 tasks per profession, a judge that scores hedged multiple-answer items as zero, and updated environments.

about.notes: The Mercor launch post (24 March 2026) gives the builders (Mercor with Cognition, which reviewed a subset of tasks), the task counts, the two domains and the Pass@1 metric; it does not explain the grading mechanics. Effort level and agent scaffold move the score, so values from different dates are not one series.
about.what_it_tests: APEX-SWE tests whether an AI agent can do production software engineering work. Its 200 hidden tasks (plus a 50-task open development set) were written by working software engineers and split evenly between integration tasks, building end-to-end systems across cloud services, business applications and infrastructure-as-code, and observability tasks, diagnosing production failures from logs, dashboards and other unstructured context. Each task has validation tests and a gold-standard output, and the result is reported as Pass@1, the first-attempt success rate.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: created by François Chollet; co-founded by Mike Knoop. The foundational paper is François Chollet's 'On the measure of intelligence' (arXiv 1911.01547, 2019). The arcprize.org page for ARC-AGI-1 was not fetched in this run, so the grid-puzzle format is stated from general knowledge, not from a source read here. Printed label says OpenAI, which is not the maintainer; the attribution appears to reflect that OpenAI's model results are reported on it.
about.what_it_tests: ARC-AGI-1 is a set of colored grid puzzles where the model sees a few input and output examples and must work out the rule for a new input. Its creator designed it to measure how efficiently a system learns a new skill from very few examples, rather than how much it has memorised. It was the first of the ARC-AGI series and was not beaten by AI systems for about five years after it appeared.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: ARC Prize; co-founded by François Chollet and Mike Knoop. Launched 2025-03-24 per the ARC Prize announcements summarised in search results. Printed labels say Google and OpenAI, but these labs are only the companies whose models are scored on it; ARC Prize maintains it. A later figure of 68.8 percent for Claude Opus 4.6 came from an unverified wiki and is not used.
about.what_it_tests: ARC-AGI-2 is a harder successor to ARC-AGI-1 that keeps the same kind of puzzle but is built so that brute-force compute does not solve it. It measures how well a system learns new rules from a few examples. At launch in March 2025, human testers averaged about 60 percent, while leading AI reasoning models scored about 1 percent.

about.notes: Launched 2026-03-25 per the ARC Prize launch post. The post reports humans at 100 percent and frontier AI at 0.51 percent at launch; a DataCamp write-up gives 0.26 percent, so that figure is not used here. Printed label says OpenAI, which is not the maintainer.
about.what_it_tests: ARC-AGI-3 is the first fully interactive benchmark in the ARC series, made of hundreds of turn-based environments and thousands of game-style levels designed by human game designers. The agent gets no instructions, rules or goals, so it must explore, work out how each environment behaves and what winning means, and carry that understanding into harder levels. It measures whether a system can learn and adapt to unfamiliar situations rather than follow instructions.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 1803.05457 (March 2018). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: The AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) is a set of grade-school science multiple-choice questions; the Challenge set holds the 2,590 questions that retrieval and co-occurrence baselines both got wrong. The score is accuracy, usually few-shot.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (17 June 2024) describes the BenchBuilder pipeline. A printed value depends on the judge model, which cards usually name in the label.
about.what_it_tests: Arena-Hard tests open-ended answering on 500 hard prompts drawn from crowdsourced conversations. An LLM judge compares the model's answers with a baseline model's answers, and the score is the resulting win rate.

about.notes: The Arena blog post "WebDev Arena" (10 March 2025, updated 13 June 2025) gives the task, the voting and the Bradley-Terry scoring. The December 2024 launch and the November 2025 rename to Code Arena come from secondary coverage. Google's model cards print the rating under the label "Code Arena" with the note "Web development".
about.what_it_tests: Code Arena, earlier called WebDev Arena, is a live human-preference leaderboard for building web applications. A user submits a prompt, such as building a simple chess game, two anonymous models each generate a web app, the user interacts with both and votes for the better one (ties allowed). The votes feed a Bradley-Terry model that estimates each model's strength from pairwise results, printed as an Elo-style rating. The scope has grown from single pages to multi-file applications, dashboards, browser games and editing tools.

about.notes: The methodology page lists v1.0 in May to June 2026 and says v1.5 is current, replacing Terminal-Bench 2.1 with Terminal-Bench 4.0 and upgrading DeepSWE to v1.1. The family label 'v1.4' is therefore superseded. The 'printed by OpenAI' label is not confirmed; comparison pages pair the index with Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build.
about.what_it_tests: The Coding Agent Index is a single score from Artificial Analysis for coding agents, meaning full tool setups such as Claude Code or Codex rather than models alone. It is an equal-weight average of benchmark components, which at v1.4 were DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas-QnA, a test of answering questions by tracing a code repository. Each component is scored as pass@1 averaged over three attempts per task, and reward-hacked or time-limited attempts score zero.

about.notes: The job label says v4.1.1, but the methodology page fetched on 2026-10-14 names v4.3.2 as current and its version history was not readable. The year is from a secondary source saying v4 launched in January 2026. Both OpenAI and xAI print this index, so the label is a third-party index that the labs cite, not their own test.
about.what_it_tests: The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index combines several test suites of primarily text-based, English-language tasks into one score for a language model. Its methodology page groups the evaluations into agents, coding, general knowledge and scientific reasoning, with a weight for each. The score is a weighted average, and agent tests are converted from Elo ratings to a 0 to 1 contribution.

about.notes: Known only from the Inkling card label.
about.what_it_tests: Audio MC is printed on the Thinking Machines Inkling model card as an audio multiple-choice evaluation; the card does not name its source or composition.

about.maintainer: AutoLogi authors (Qin Zhu and co-authors, Fudan University and Alibaba)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2502.16906 (February 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: AutoLogi tests logical reasoning with automatically generated open-ended logic puzzles in English and Chinese, where each puzzle comes with a program that verifies any proposed solution, so answers are checked exactly rather than by multiple choice. The score is accuracy over the puzzles.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (paper authors Daniel Shepard and Robin Salimans); Artificial Analysis runs the AutomationBench-AA leaderboard in partnership with Zapier. The benchmark has several versions and scores differ by version and source: the Zapier public leaderboard, the Artificial Analysis guardrail-based AutomationBench-AA (657 private tasks, announced July 6, 2026), and BenchLM private-set figures are not comparable. The arXiv abstract says even the best frontier models scored below 10 percent at release. The printed-by labels (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Alibaba) were not checked against model cards.
about.what_it_tests: AutomationBench tests whether AI agents can carry out business workflows that span several software applications, such as a CRM, an inbox, a calendar and a messaging tool, through their REST APIs. The agent has to find the right endpoints on its own, follow layered business rules, and ignore misleading records along the way. Grading is programmatic: the final state of the simulated systems is checked against success criteria, so a run is judged on the end result.

about.notes: Named on the Mistral Large 4 release page (October 2026) as the public B3 AI Security Benchmark. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: The B3 (Backbone Breaker) AI Security Benchmark from Lakera attacks an LLM agent backbone with prompt-injection and related attacks drawn from its Gandalf red-teaming game; the score printed is the share of attacks resisted, so higher is better.

about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 10 January 2026, revised 7 July 2026; ICML 2026) gives the item count, the 22 subclasses, the four-category structure and the human comparison; the four category names and the UniPat AI affiliation come from secondary coverage. "With tools" on a model card is the publisher's setup note, not part of the benchmark definition.
about.what_it_tests: BabyVision tests core visual abilities that do not depend on language: basic visual tasks that young children solve, grouped into four categories (fine-grained discrimination, visual tracking, spatial perception and visual pattern recognition) across 388 items in 22 subclasses. Scores are accuracy against human baselines; the paper reports the best model at 49.7 against an adult average of 94.1.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (26 February 2025, Mehran Kazemi and co-authors) describes the task replacement and the harmonic-average score. A model card that prints one percentage does not say whether it is the harmonic or the plain average.
about.what_it_tests: BIG-Bench Extra Hard (BBEH) tests general reasoning. Every task of the earlier BIG-Bench Hard is replaced by a new task that targets the same skill at a much higher difficulty, so that current models no longer saturate it. The score is accuracy; the paper reports a harmonic average over tasks.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (17 October 2022) describes the task selection. BIG-Bench Extra Hard is a separate, harder successor.
about.what_it_tests: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) is a set of 23 BIG-Bench tasks on which earlier models scored below the average human rater, many of them needing multi-step reasoning. The score is accuracy, usually with three-shot chain-of-thought prompting.

about.maintainer: Authors of the May 2026 arXiv paper
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (listed as Haozhe Zhang, Kaichen Liu and Hanjie Chen by an aggregator); a host organisation is not confirmed, and no OpenAI link was found. The job label says OpenAI prints this benchmark, but I found only the academic arXiv paper and no OpenAI publication or card that uses it, so the printed attribution is unconfirmed. Independent leaderboard numbers were not found.
about.what_it_tests: BenchCAD is a benchmark of 17,900 industrial CAD programs written in CadQuery, each checked by running it, across 106 part families such as gears, springs and drill bits. Models answer questions about drawings and code, turn an image into code, and edit code according to an instruction. The authors report that current models often capture the rough outer shape of a part but struggle to build faithful parametric programs.

about.notes: Dataset card (2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: BeyondAIME is a set of 100 competition-style mathematics problems written to be harder than AIME and free of memorised answers. The score is the share solved, usually averaged over several samples (avg@16).

about.maintainer: UC Berkeley Gorilla project (Shishir G. Patil and co-authors)
about.notes: The leaderboard page describes the versions and the scoring; the accompanying paper appeared at ICML 2025.
about.what_it_tests: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) tests whether a model produces correct function calls from a tool description and a request. Version 3 added multi-turn interactions checked by the resulting system state; version 4 added agentic evaluation. Overall accuracy is the unweighted average of the sub-categories.

about.notes: Rogo announced the benchmark on 27 May 2026 and the arXiv paper (submitted 3 June 2026) lists authors from Rogo and OpenAI. Rubric scores and final-answer scores are different numbers; a page that prints one figure without saying which is read as it stands.
about.what_it_tests: BigFinanceBench tests whether an AI agent can do the research work of a professional financial analyst. Each of its 928 questions comes with a reference answer and a rubric that breaks the derivation into steps that can be checked one by one, so partial credit follows the analyst workflow rather than the final number alone. A 50-question subset is public; the full set stays private.

about.maintainer: BigCode project (Terry Yue Zhuo and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (22 June 2024) describes the tasks and the test coverage.
about.what_it_tests: BigCodeBench tests code generation with 1,140 Python tasks that need calls into 139 libraries across seven domains, each checked by several unit tests. The score is the share of tasks whose generated code passes all tests.

about.notes: The Anthropic research post (29 April 2026) gives the counts, the two splits and the grading. The Human Difficult split started at 27 and lost 4 malformed questions. The Hugging Face release (Anthropic/BioMysteryBench-full) lists 90 problems after an answer-key audit removed 9 and edited 24, so a published value may rest on either revision unless the publisher says which. Anthropic's own values appear in its system cards under life-sciences capabilities.
about.what_it_tests: BioMysteryBench tests whether a model can do real bioinformatics research work on messy real-world data. Domain experts wrote 99 questions, each built from a dataset and a controlled, objective property of that data, so every answer has an objective ground truth. Grading looks at the final answer only. The questions are split into Human Solvable (76: at least one of up to five domain experts answered it from scratch) and Human Difficult (23: no expert on the panel solved it), and publishers report the two splits separately; each problem is attempted five times and accuracy is averaged.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (San Francisco company); xAI prints the scores in its Grok 4.6 reporting. Refusal paper is arXiv 2607.05462; Surveillance is arXiv 2607.19262; Function is a preprint listed on Sciety (doi 10.64898/2026.09.03.749010). The xAI Grok 4.6 post (x.ai/news/biosafety-at-the-frontier) names BioSecBench-Refusal and BioSecBench-Surveillance and gives scores for Grok 4.6; the post is the source for the xAI attribution. Scores are not repeated here because they are vendor-reported.
about.what_it_tests: BioSecBench is a family of three checkable tests from LatchBio for AI agents doing biology work with a biosecurity angle. The Refusal part pairs routine research tasks with tasks that look like research but hide a hazard, and measures how often an agent refuses. The Surveillance part checks whether an agent can run pathogen genomic surveillance analyses correctly, and the Function part checks whether an agent can infer biological function from experimental data, scored against ground truth.

about.maintainer: SecureBio and Center for AI Safety (authors of the Virology Capabilities Test paper)
about.notes: The public VCT paper (arXiv 2504.16137, first submitted 2025-04-21) was read. The 'Biosecurity VCT' subset and its xAI-card score are not in the paper, and an aggregator says the exact subset is not exposed, so attribution of the subset is unconfirmed. The question format is not settled: the paper page does not state it, and a secondary paper (arXiv 2505.06108) describes the text-only subset as multiple-response. The Grok card PDF was not readable here. No scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: The Virology Capabilities Test measures whether a model can troubleshoot complex virology lab protocols. It has 322 multimodal questions covering fundamental, tacit and visual knowledge, written from the inputs of dozens of PhD-level expert virologists. Results are reported as accuracy, and the paper compares them with expert virologists who had internet access. The biosecurity subset printed on the xAI card is not described in the paper.

about.notes: No primary source found. The closest published items are BioTIER (arXiv 2607.14479, 542 expert-curated prompts), BioSecBench-Refusal (LatchBio, arXiv 2607.05462) and RefusalBench (arXiv 2605.21545). None is named BioUseBench, so the name may be a mislabel of one of them; that is not confirmed. The xAI Grok 4.7 card PDF was not readable, so the printed label is unconfirmed.
about.what_it_tests: BioUseBench is printed as a dual-use refusal test for biology, which would score how often a model declines biology requests that could help research or cause harm. No published description of its prompts, design or scoring under this name was found. One aggregator lists a refusal figure for an xAI model card, and that figure is not used here.

about.notes: Announced March 2025 (paper Mitchener et al., arXiv 2503.00096). The original paper reported 17% open-answer accuracy for Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The catalog label zero-shot MCQ accuracy refers to the multiple-choice grading mode. Later subset results (BixBench-Verified-50) are self-reported by vendors and are not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: BixBench tests whether AI agents can do realistic bioinformatics analysis. The benchmark has 53 analysis scenarios built from published research notebooks, with 296 questions in total. An agent receives the data and must run the analysis and answer, and answers are graded either open-ended or as multiple choice.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (September 2025) describes the first version and its scoring; the agent-only second version with normalized scores is described on the Andon Labs page (andonlabs.com/evals/blueprint-bench-2). Google model cards print Blueprint-Bench 2 as a percentage with the note "Normalized score".
about.what_it_tests: Blueprint-Bench tests spatial reasoning by asking a model to turn photographs of an apartment into a two-dimensional floor plan. The plan is scored against the true one by comparing which rooms connect and how their sizes rank. Blueprint-Bench 2 is the agent-only version: an agent works through 50 apartments in sequence and keeps a notepad between them, and its score is normalized so that a random plan scores 0 and a perfect one scores 1.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: Jason Wei, Zhiqing Sun and about eight other OpenAI co-authors. Released April 2025; the paper is arXiv 2504.12516. Official data is distributed through OpenAI's simple-evals repository in encrypted form. Printed labels Google and xAI are not confirmed by any source found; they are presumably companies that report results on it.
about.what_it_tests: BrowseComp tests whether an AI agent with web browsing can find hard-to-locate facts that are spread across many sources and tied together. It has 1,266 questions with short answers that are easy to check against a reference. Models without browsing scored near zero when it was released, and a browsing agent solved about half of the questions.

about.notes: OpenAI release pages print it under Long context with the context length in the label and give no separate methodology page; the description here is inferred from the name and the placement and was not checked against a primary source.
about.what_it_tests: BrowseComp Long Context takes questions from BrowseComp, the OpenAI browsing benchmark of hard-to-find facts, and places the web content needed to answer them inside the prompt instead of behind a search tool, at a stated context length (128k or 256k tokens). It measures whether a model can find and combine the relevant pieces of a long context rather than whether it can search.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (27 April 2025) describes the question construction.
about.what_it_tests: BrowseComp-ZH tests web browsing on the Chinese internet with 289 multi-hop questions across 11 domains, each built backwards from a short objective answer. The score is accuracy.

about.maintainer: Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Tsinghua University (Yuzhen Huang and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (15 May 2023) describes the levels and disciplines.
about.what_it_tests: C-Eval tests knowledge and reasoning in Chinese with multiple-choice questions from 52 disciplines at four levels: middle school, high school, college and professional. The score is accuracy over the question set.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (the benchmark sits in the huggingface GitHub organisation); xAI prints the scores. Leaderboard figures in aggregators conflict across snapshots, so no score is given here; the official Hugging Face leaderboard is the place to check. The reward label printed by xAI is not explained by the repository.
about.what_it_tests: CADGenBench judges whether AI systems can produce usable 3D mechanical parts. It has two tasks: build a valid, geometrically correct 3D model from an engineering drawing, and edit an existing STEP file to apply a requested change. Each sample gets one STEP or BREP file, and scoring runs on a leaderboard against ground truth that stays private.

about.notes: No maintainer page, paper or repository was found. The printed label says xAI, but the xAI Grok 4.7 launch page does not mention CathedralBench, and the same aggregator lists the developer as SpaceXAI, a discrepancy that is unresolved. The aggregator's score figures are not used. Maintainer and url stay null until a primary source is found.
about.what_it_tests: CathedralBench is described by one third-party tracker as a cyber challenge in which an agent must chain several exploits to get through a hardened system. Results are reported only on the hardest tasks, and the runs are without safeguards, to show what the underlying model can do when it is not restricted. This description is secondhand and was not checked against a primary source. No scores are given.

about.maintainer: Alibaba (Qwen team; Zhibo Yang and co-authors)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2412.02210 (December 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: CC-OCR tests OCR-centred reading in four tracks: multi-scene text reading, multilingual text reading, document parsing and key information extraction, over 39 subsets with 7,058 images in which about 41% were not public before. The score is an average over the tracks of their native metrics.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: authors Suhaas Garre, Chris Mutty, Sushant Mehta and Edwin Chen; the Hugging Face dataset is under the surgeai namespace. arXiv 2608.10677, submitted August 11, 2026. The paper reports mean pass@1 over 30 model configurations with 20 trials per task. The arXiv page does not describe how an individual answer is judged beyond the expert ranges. The 'with tools' variant is a catalog label; aggregators report it, and the paper's tool setup was not confirmed here.
about.what_it_tests: Chartography tests whether AI models can read and reason about professional charts, such as Kaplan-Meier survival curves, candlestick charts, Sankey diagrams and Bode plots, which standard chart tests rarely include. It has 100 tasks written by professionals in fields such as medicine, engineering, finance and manufacturing. Numeric answers are checked against ranges set by the expert author, and scores are averaged over repeated runs.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2203.10244 (March 2022). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: ChartQA asks questions about chart images that need visual reading and arithmetic or logical reasoning, with human-written and machine-generated question sets. The score is relaxed accuracy on the test split.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2504.05506 (April 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: ChartQAPro is the harder successor of ChartQA: 1,341 charts from 157 sources with 1,948 questions of several types (multiple choice, conversational, hypothetical, unanswerable), many needing multi-step visual reasoning. The score is accuracy.

about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 26 June 2024, lead author Zirui Wang) gives the chart count, the two question types and the expert curation. The abstract does not say how accuracy is computed; "no tools" on a model card is the publisher's setup note, not part of the benchmark definition. Published at NeurIPS 2024 (secondary coverage).
about.what_it_tests: CharXiv tests whether a multimodal model can read real scientific charts. The set holds 2,323 charts taken from arXiv papers, each with descriptive questions about basic chart elements and reasoning questions that need information synthesized across the chart. All charts and questions were hand-picked and verified by human experts. The reasoning split, the one model cards report, is scored as accuracy on the reasoning questions.

about.maintainer: Taobao and Tmall Group (Yancheng He and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (11 November 2024) describes the topics and the grading. Cards print it as Chinese-SimpleQA or C-SimpleQA.
about.what_it_tests: Chinese SimpleQA tests factual recall in Chinese with short questions across six topics and 99 subtopics. An LLM grader marks each answer correct or not, and the score is the share answered correctly.

about.maintainer: Claw-Eval team (project linked to PKU and HKU; the README names Lei Li of HKU as project lead)
about.notes: The text split of Claw-Eval; the multimodal split is the separate ClawEval-MM family. The Kimi K2.6 card ran version 1.1 with max-tokens-per-step 16384. Maintainer detail copied from the ClawEval-MM record; the repository was not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: Claw-Eval is an end-to-end evaluation suite for LLM agents on multi-step software workflows: the agent has to finish realistic tasks inside tool environments, and a task counts only when the end state is right. Model cards print two readings of the same runs: pass@3, the share of tasks solved in at least one of three attempts, and pass^3, the share solved in all three, which rewards consistency.

about.maintainer: Not stated on the pages read
about.notes: Known only from the StepFun Step 3.7 Flash model card. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: ClawEval scores an agent on multi-turn tool orchestration tasks with adversarial traps and system policies to respect; the page reporting it (StepFun) cites version 1.1 dated 2026-05-09 and reports a 0 to 100 score.

about.maintainer: Claw-Eval team (project linked to PKU and HKU; the README names Lei Li of HKU as project lead; paper lead author Bowen Ye)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (v1 submitted 7 April 2026, lead author Bowen Ye, v3 revised 7 May 2026) gives the 101-task multimodal split and the Pass@k, Pass^k and average-score definitions. Neither the paper text read nor the GitHub README uses the name ClawEval-MM, so the label used on model cards is not confirmed; the multimodal split of Claw-Eval is the closest primary match. The README names Pass^3 as its primary metric, and only the paper defines Pass@3 and average score.
about.what_it_tests: The multimodal split of Claw-Eval, an end-to-end evaluation suite for LLM agents on multi-step software workflows, tests whether a model can complete perception and creation tasks. The README describes the split as covering webpage generation, video QA and document extraction. The paper states that the split holds 101 tasks across three domains: video (53), document and image (22) and code (26). Grading covers completion, safety and robustness and uses execution traces, audit logs and environment snapshots. The paper defines Pass@k as the fraction of tasks passed at least once in k runs, average score as the mean over all runs, and Pass^k as the fraction of tasks passed on every trial.

about.maintainer: CLUE benchmark team (Liang Xu and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (13 April 2020) describes the nine CLUE tasks; the Winograd task is one of them. Model cards print it on its own as CLUEWSC.
about.what_it_tests: CLUEWSC is the Winograd Schema task of the CLUE Chinese language understanding benchmark: the model decides which noun a pronoun in a Chinese sentence refers to. The score is accuracy.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (29 June 2023) describes the grades and the distractor test.
about.what_it_tests: CMATH tests elementary-school math in Chinese with about 1,700 word problems from workbooks and exams across six grades. The score is accuracy, which the paper also reports per grade.

about.maintainer: MBZUAI and partners (Haonan Li and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (15 June 2023) describes the subjects and the few-shot and chain-of-thought settings.
about.what_it_tests: CMMLU tests knowledge and reasoning in Chinese across natural sciences, social sciences, engineering and the humanities, in the multiple-choice format of MMLU. The score is accuracy; random guessing scores 25 percent.

about.maintainer: Chinese Mathematical Society (competition); evaluation sets assembled by model publishers
about.notes: There is no benchmark paper; DeepSeek model cards print "CNMO 2024 (Pass@1)" without saying how the problems were graded.
about.what_it_tests: CNMO 2024 is the problem set of the 2024 Chinese National Mathematical Olympiad used as a math test: the model must produce the final answers to the competition problems. The score is the share answered correctly.

about.notes: Written from the printed label and general knowledge of the platform. The card does not say which contests, how many attempts or what method produced the rating, and no maintainer page describes an evaluation protocol for models.
about.what_it_tests: Codeforces is a competitive programming platform whose contestants hold an Elo-style rating updated after each rated contest. A model developer who prints a "Codeforces rating" has estimated where the model would stand on that scale from its results on contest problems.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2307.08689 (July 2023). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: COLLIE is a grammar-based framework for compositional constraints on generated text: word-, sentence- and paragraph-level constraints (counts, positions, included or excluded words) that the model must satisfy exactly. The score is the share of constraints satisfied.

about.notes: The Vals AI benchmark page (updated 12 August 2026) gives the question counts, judge, metric and archive status, but gives no release or introduction date and links no research paper, so the introduction year is left null. The 858-question figure is the private test set; the public validation set has 20 questions from one document. The BenchLM mirror snapshots in search results were not used as sources.
about.what_it_tests: CorpFin (CorpFin v2) tests whether a model can answer questions about long-context credit agreements, contracts that are often over 200 pages long. Questions cover extracting terms and numbers, summarizing, numeric reasoning, cross-referencing earlier definitions, judging terms against market standards and understanding industry jargon. The private test set has 858 questions from 43 documents, written by Vals AI with financial analysts, legal professionals and academics. Answers are graded by an Anthropic model as the LLM judge at temperature 0, under three context setups (Exact Pages, Shared Max Context and Max Fitting Context). The printed metric is accuracy, as a percentage, and the benchmark is now archived because performance has saturated.

about.maintainer: Alibaba Tongyi Lab (Zhiyuan Lu and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (21 January 2026) describes the synthetic queries and programmatic answers; its abstract does not fix one metric, so a printed value keeps the metric label the publisher used.
about.what_it_tests: CorpusQA tests reasoning over whole document collections: the evidence for a question is spread over hundreds of files, and the answer needs comparison or aggregation rather than lookup. Inputs scale up to about 10 million tokens; publishers usually print the 1 million token setting as accuracy.

about.maintainer: Roni Paiss and co-authors (Google Research and Tel Aviv University), from the "Teaching CLIP to Count to Ten" work
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2302.12066 (ICCV 2023). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: CountBench is a counting benchmark of 540 images, each with a caption naming between two and ten objects of one kind, built from LAION-400M. A model is asked how many instances appear, and the score is accuracy over the images.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (20 July 2020, Changhan Wang and co-authors) describes the language pairs; its abstract does not name the metric, so the unit of a printed value is taken from the publisher's own note.
about.what_it_tests: CoVoST 2 tests speech-to-text translation: the model hears speech and writes its translation. The corpus covers translation from 21 languages into English and from English into 15 other languages, built on Common Voice recordings. Publishers usually report BLEU, the standard translation score, but a model card that prints one number does not always name the metric.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Qwen team), as named in the Qwen3.8 model card. All scores are vendor-reported and the card says results come from Qwen's own testing. No independent evaluation or paper was found. The year is inferred from the Qwen3.8 release, not from a stated introduction date. BenchLM figures (75.3 and 74.8) are secondary and were not checked against the card.
about.what_it_tests: CoWorkBench is an in-house Qwen benchmark for long-horizon professional work across computer science, finance, law, medicine and other productivity domains. Its grading method is not published.

about.maintainer: CritPt research team (lead author Minhui Zhu); Artificial Analysis runs the public leaderboard evaluation
about.notes: The arXiv abstract (v1 submitted 30 September 2025, first author Minhui Zhu, listed version v4 revised 8 May 2026) gives the challenge and checkpoint counts, the authorship, the grading approach and average accuracy; the Artificial Analysis evaluation page gives the 'CritPt: Score' label and says the benchmark is 'under review by its authors following external feedback', with scores expected to change on a revised dataset. Artificial Analysis runs 70 test problems without an agent harness, and the accuracy figure it quotes for the best base model (4.0%) differs from the 5.7% in the v4 abstract, so state the version or source with any number.
about.what_it_tests: CritPt tests whether a language model can solve research-level physics problems of the kind a working physicist meets in a research project. The benchmark has 71 composite research challenges, each split into simpler checkpoint tasks (190 in total), across areas such as condensed matter, quantum physics, astrophysics, high energy physics and biophysics. All problems are new and were written by more than 50 active physics researchers from their own research. Each answer is hand-curated to be guess-resistant and machine-checkable, and the main metric is average accuracy, shown on Artificial Analysis as the 'CritPt: Score' percentage.

about.notes: The page's changelog starts with version 3.0 on March 11, 2026, and version 4.0 is dated September 10, 2026. Scores are only comparable within one version. Cursor's page and its mirrors show different leaders for different snapshots. The 'printed by Anthropic, xAI' labels were not confirmed.
about.what_it_tests: CursorBench is Cursor's own coding-agent benchmark, built from ambiguous, multi-file tasks taken from real Cursor sessions. Version 4.0 adds long-horizon work such as editing, refactoring, investigation and managing jobs. Each agent gets a percentage score, and the page also reports cost per task and tokens used.

about.maintainer: Yuxuan Zhu, Daniel Kang and co-authors
about.notes: Maintainer detail: paper published at ICML 2025. Printed label says xAI. The xAI Grok 4.7 launch page does not mention CVE-Bench, so the xAI attribution is unconfirmed. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists CVE-Bench as a cyber evaluation that was retired after it became saturated, so the name appears in OpenAI's card too.
about.what_it_tests: CVE-Bench measures whether AI agents can succeed against 40 real, serious web application vulnerabilities taken from the US national vulnerability database. The targets are content management systems and AI applications, and each attempt is checked automatically inside a sandbox. The paper's headline finding is that the best agent framework succeeded on up to 13 percent of the vulnerabilities.

about.notes: Maintainer and method are from the cwe-bench.com page, which cites Collinear AI as author and names Artificial Analysis as the independent evaluator that ran the published results. The page lists v0 on Sept 1 and v1 on Sept 25, and its citations give 2026, which is where the year comes from. The printed label says Google, and no Google source was found, so that attribution is unconfirmed; an aggregator naming a Google model as top scorer is a leaderboard fact, not a maintainer fact. The page has no separate paper. The v1 three-judge panel is reported beside the deterministic score, not in place of it. No scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: CWE-Bench evaluates coding agents on defensive security work. Each task gives the agent a checkout of a real open-source repository, sometimes with disclosed CVEs reproduced in it, and asks it to audit the code and fix what it finds without being told how many vulnerabilities there are. A fix counts only if the exploit is blocked and the existing tests still pass, with no partial credit, and agents are not asked to write exploits. The page reports 100 held-out tasks in v0 and 120 in v1.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2408.08926 (August 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: Cybench is a set of 40 professional-level capture-the-flag tasks from four recent security competitions (HackTheBox, Sekai CTF, Glacier, HKCert), run by an agent in a sandbox; a task counts when the agent recovers the flag, and subtasks give partial credit. The score is the share of tasks solved.

about.notes: Defined on the Mistral Large 4 release page (October 2026). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: The average refusal rate on malicious cybersecurity prompts drawn from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, as computed by Mistral AI; higher means more harmful requests refused.

about.maintainer: UC Berkeley Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Berkeley RDI); authors Zhun Wang, Tianneng Shi, Jingxuan He, Matthew Cai, Jialin Zhang and Dawn Song. The paper (arXiv 2506.02548, first posted June 2025) was published at ICLR 2026. Printed label says xAI, and the xAI Grok 4.7 launch page does not mention CyberGym, so that attribution is unconfirmed. The RDI page links a live observatory at https://rdi.berkeley.edu/frontier-ai-impact-on-cybersecurity/benchmarks.html for leaderboard results.
about.what_it_tests: CyberGym tests whether AI agents can reproduce real vulnerabilities in open-source software. The agent gets a vulnerable codebase and a written description, and must write a test input that makes the bug crash the code before the fix but not after it. The benchmark has 1,507 vulnerabilities across 188 open-source projects, and each attempt is checked automatically with sanitizers.

about.maintainer: DeepPlanning authors (published with the Qwen3.5 evaluations)
about.notes: Appears on the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 model cards without a note. The maintainer and the public release were not confirmed for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: DeepPlanning tests long-horizon planning by an agent: tasks such as trip planning that need many tool calls, constraint tracking and a final plan that satisfies every requirement. The score is the share of tasks whose final plan passes the checks; the Qwen cards print one number per model.

about.maintainer: Google (paper authors from Google DeepMind, Google Search, Kaggle and Google Research, per the arXiv listing; first author Nikita Gupta)
about.notes: The arXiv paper 2601.20975 (submitted 28 January 2026, first author Nikita Gupta) gives the 900 tasks, the 17 fields and, in Section 3.1 of the HTML version, F1 as the primary ranking metric along with the Fully Correct definition. The abstract page names only recall and precision, and the Parallel blog page reports accuracy and cost rather than F1, so the F1 statement rests on the full text. Kaggle leaderboard figures and vendor-reported scores were not checked.
about.what_it_tests: DeepSearchQA tests whether a deep research agent can finish an open-ended information-seeking task by finding every item in an answer set, not a single fact. The benchmark has 900 multi-step tasks across 17 fields, and the agent has to search, collate fragmented information from different sources, remove duplicates and decide when the search is complete. The submitted answer set is compared with the ground-truth set, and the primary ranking metric is F1, the harmonic mean of precision and recall computed per prompt and then averaged, with a binary 'Fully Correct' outcome for an exact set match.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: authors Wenqi Huang, Charley Lee, Leonard Tng and Serena Ge. The fetched launch post (May 26, 2026) describes v1.0. The page links to v1.1 as the latest version, which this description does not cover. The 'printed by Google, OpenAI, xAI, Alibaba' labels were not verified in model cards.
about.what_it_tests: DeepSWE tests whether coding agents can make original, long-horizon software engineering changes in real open-source repositories. It has 113 tasks across 91 repositories in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript and Rust, all written from scratch so that solutions are not copied from existing commits. Hand-written verifiers check behavior through public interfaces, and each verifier runs three times to catch flakiness.

about.maintainer: Not stated on the page read
about.notes: Known only from the Mistral Large 4 release page (October 2026). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: Dense200 tests visual grounding in dense natural scenes: the model has to localise many objects in one image, and the bbox variant scores the predicted bounding boxes. The Mistral Large 4 page prints it as a percentage.

about.maintainer: Minesh Mathew and co-authors (IIIT Hyderabad and CVC)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2007.00398 (July 2020). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: DocVQA is visual question answering over scanned document images (forms, letters, reports). The score is ANLS (average normalised Levenshtein similarity), printed as a 0-100 number.

about.maintainer: Allen Institute for AI and UC Irvine (Dheeru Dua and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (1 March 2019) describes the operations and the F1 score.
about.what_it_tests: DROP tests reading comprehension that needs discrete reasoning over a paragraph: resolving references, then adding, counting, comparing or sorting what the paragraph says. The score is a token-level F1 between the answer and the reference, printed as a percentage.

about.notes: The only description is the footnote on the DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 and V4-Flash-0731 model cards.
about.what_it_tests: DSBench is a pair of internal DeepSeek test sets: DSBench-FullStack holds full-stack development tasks and DSBench-Hard holds difficult coding-agent problems. The tasks and the scoring are not published.

about.maintainer: Chengke Zou and co-authors (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and UC Berkeley)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2411.00836 (ICLR 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry. Qwen cards print one number without naming which accuracy.
about.what_it_tests: DynaMath tests how robust the visual mathematical reasoning of a model is: 501 seed questions are each generated as a program that can vary the numbers, graphs or figures, giving many concrete variants of the same problem. The usual score is average accuracy over the generated variants; a worst-case accuracy over the variants of each seed is also defined.

about.notes: Maintainer and method come from atopile's own EEBench methodology page, which says the benchmark is built and funded by atopile and that its V1 tasks were written in 2026 and kept private. No release year is stated, so introduced is null. The printed label says xAI; no xAI source was readable, so that relation is unconfirmed. Do not confuse with EEE-Bench (CVPR 2025), a separate benchmark. An aggregator's description of a physics-simulation framework conflicts with the project page and was not used. No scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: EEBench is an agent benchmark for electrical and hardware engineering, aimed at the requirements, design and test loop of a hardware project. Agents submit atopile design bundles, and the harness builds the circuit graph, bill of materials and simulation decks from that source. Each requirement is checked by simulation at worst-case component-tolerance corners, and the leaderboard score blends engineering results at 65% with cost efficiency at 35% against a reference bill of materials. The held-out tasks are not published.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2406.05756 (ACL 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: EmbSpatial-Bench tests spatial understanding from an embodied, egocentric point of view: multiple-choice questions about six spatial relations (above, below, left, right, close, far) between objects in indoor scenes drawn from embodied simulation environments. The score is accuracy.

about.notes: Defined on the Jamba2 release page (January 2026). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: The Enterprise Reliability Score is an average that AI21 Labs publishes over its instruction-following benchmarks (IFBench, COLLIE, IFEval) and the FACTS grounding benchmark; it summarises steerability and context faithfulness on one 0 to 1 scale.

about.maintainer: Google DeepMind (Gemini Robotics team); the repository sits under the embodiedreasoning organisation
about.notes: The GitHub README (CC-BY-4.0 licence) gives the 400-example count, the multiple-choice format and the TF Example data file, and it ties the release to the Gemini Robotics work. The README gives no release date; 2025 comes from arXiv 2503.20020 (submitted 25 March 2025, credited to the Gemini Robotics Team), whose abstract does not name ERQA itself. A different benchmark, ERQA-Plus (arXiv 2606.17639), appeared in search results only and is not the same set.
about.what_it_tests: ERQA is a multimodal benchmark of embodied reasoning questions for robotics-related scenarios. The README says it covers spatial reasoning and world knowledge, and each item mixes images and text in a multiple-choice question with answers labelled A to D. The full benchmark consists of 400 examples. The README does not list named reasoning categories, and its evaluation harness queries the Gemini and OpenAI APIs; the README gives no accuracy formula beyond the ground-truth letter answer per question.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: Carnegie Mellon University per secondary coverage; affiliations not shown on the arXiv page. Printed label says OpenAI, which does not match the public benchmark: its authors are academic, and the arXiv paper was posted 2026-05-13. The GPT-6 Astra system card (https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra/) lists ExploitBench and a separate 'ExploitBench - Internal Port (June-August 2026)' that uses only vulnerabilities disclosed after the model's knowledge cutoff. The internal port is OpenAI-only; the public benchmark is not.
about.what_it_tests: ExploitBench measures how far an AI agent gets along a ladder of 16 checkable capability steps when it works on known, already-patched bugs in the V8 JavaScript engine used by Chromium. The steps run from triggering the bug up to full control of the target, and each step is confirmed by an automatic verifier with no AI judge. The public set has 41 bugs, all reported in 2024 or later.

about.maintainer: Academic author team led by UC Berkeley researchers
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Zhun Wang, Dawn Song and co-authors) with contributors from several universities; secondary coverage also lists staff from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google among the co-authors. Printed label says OpenAI. The arXiv page does not show affiliations, and the lead team is academic, so OpenAI is not the maintainer. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists ExploitGym as an OpenAI cyber evaluation and a separate honeypot test built on it, so OpenAI does use it. The preprint date is 2026-05-11 on arXiv; a secondary write-up cites 2026-07-22 for results, which is not used here.
about.what_it_tests: ExploitGym measures whether AI agents can take a program input that already triggers a software vulnerability and turn it step by step into a working attack. The benchmark has 898 instances in three areas: ordinary user programs, a JavaScript engine, and the Linux kernel. Protections are varied from task to task to see how they change agent success, and every task runs in a reproducible container.

about.notes: Section 8.2.3 of the GPT-6 Astra system card names the evaluation, and the printed label matches its title. The catalog dates the card 2026-09-03, which is where the year comes from. The card was searched in three passes and its final part was partly unavailable; the honeypot section is in the part read. The public base benchmark is arXiv 2605.11086 (submitted 2026-05-11), a separate paper that does not mention a honeypot. No scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: The honeypot evaluation appears in the GPT-6 Astra system card as 'Declining to Exploit a Honeypot During Difficult ExploitGym Problems'. The model works hard ExploitGym tasks, which ask it to turn a vulnerability-triggering input into a working exploit, and an out-of-scope flag is planted where it could be attacked. The score is the share of adversarial cases in which the model attacks the honeypot, so lower is better. The base ExploitGym benchmark has 898 instances drawn from userspace programs, Google's V8 engine and the Linux kernel.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2501.03200 (December 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: FACTS Grounding asks the model to answer a request using only a supplied document of up to 32k tokens; judge models check that each response is fully grounded in the document and still answers the request. The score is the share of responses judged grounded.

about.notes: The Google DeepMind announcement (9 December 2025) describes the four parts of the suite; Kaggle holds the private sets and the leaderboard. A model card that prints "FACTS Parametric" with a shot count ran the public set itself.
about.what_it_tests: FACTS Parametric is the closed-book part of the FACTS Benchmark Suite: trivia-style factual questions that a model must answer from its own knowledge, without search or other tools. It has public and private question sets of 1,052 items each, and the score is accuracy.

about.maintainer: Min et al. (University of Washington and collaborators)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2305.14251 (May 2023). OpenAI reports its own grading on these prompts; details in its system cards. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: FActScore scores long-form text by breaking it into atomic facts and checking each against a knowledge source; publishers report the share of unsupported facts as a hallucination rate, so lower is better.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with Stanford researchers, per the arXiv paper. The arXiv paper 2508.00828 dates the original benchmark to August 2025. The Vals page (dated October 12, 2026) says v2 builds on v1.1 and gives its scoring modes. Leaderboard figures differ by snapshot, and the 'printed by Google' label was not verified.
about.what_it_tests: Finance Agent tests AI agents on research tasks that a financial analyst would do, such as answering questions from recent SEC filings. The original version had 537 expert-written questions in nine task categories, and the agent is given search and EDGAR database access. Version 2 contains 927 expert-reviewed questions, and results are reported as partial credit or as all-pass, where a fully correct answer is required.

about.notes: Written from the arXiv listing (September 2025) as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: FinSearchComp tests search agents on realistic financial information tasks in three tiers: T1 time-sensitive data fetching, T2 simple historical lookup and T3 complex historical investigation, across global and Greater China markets. Answers are checked against expert-verified references; the score is accuracy. Model cards often print only the T2 and T3 tiers, whose answers do not change with the date.

about.maintainer: Not stated on the page read
about.notes: The page describes it as testing spreadsheet creation and editing on real-life finance and accounting use cases. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: FinWorkBench (printed as Finch on the Mistral Large 4 page) tests whether a model can create and edit spreadsheets for real finance and accounting use cases; the score is the share of tasks completed correctly.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (25 May 2022, Alexis Conneau and co-authors) describes the corpus; its abstract does not name the metrics. A model card that prints a small decimal with "lower is better" and no metric name is stored as a fraction with that note.
about.what_it_tests: FLEURS is a multilingual speech benchmark with about 12 hours of speech in each of 102 languages, parallel across languages because it is read from the FLoRes-101 translation sentences. It is used for speech recognition, language identification, translation and retrieval. For speech recognition the usual score is the word error rate, where lower is better.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2506.14922 (June 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: FORTRESS (Frontier Risk Evaluation for National Security and Public Safety) pairs adversarial prompts in CBRNE, political violence and criminal domains with benign look-alikes, so a model is scored both on refusing harmful requests (Adversarial) and on answering benign ones (Benign). Higher is better on both.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (19 September 2024) describes the questions and the accuracy score. Publishers print the accuracy either as a fraction or as a percentage.
about.what_it_tests: FRAMES (Fact, Fetch, and Reason) tests whether a model can answer multi-hop questions that need facts from several web sources combined by reasoning. It is used to evaluate retrieval-augmented and search-agent setups. The score is the share of questions answered correctly.

about.maintainer: Not stated on the page read
about.notes: Known only from the Claude Opus 5 release page (July 2026), which runs it on the mini-SWE-agent harness. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: Frontier-Bench (v0.1 on the Anthropic Claude Opus 5 page) is a set of hard agentic terminal tasks in software and engineering work, such as rebuilding a machine part as a 3D CAD model from a drawing; the model works in a terminal harness and the score is the mean reward over several attempts per task.

about.maintainer: Cognition, built with maintainers of 36 open-source repositories
about.notes: Cognition announced the benchmark in June 2026 and released version 1.1 in July 2026. Cognition's own announcement page was not located, so the description rests on the Artificial Analysis article (published October 12, 2026). Epoch AI describes Main and Extended subsets, while the Artificial Analysis article describes only Main. The 'printed by Anthropic, OpenAI' labels were not confirmed.
about.what_it_tests: FrontierCode tests whether an AI coding agent's change to a real open-source project is good enough for that project's maintainers to merge, not just code that passes tests. It has 150 tasks drawn from 36 repositories, and Artificial Analysis runs the 100-task Main set with three attempts per task. Each attempt must pass deterministic tests and file-scope limits, and an LLM judge checks it against maintainer criteria, where failing any blocking check scores zero.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: OpenAI commissioned part of the problems and supported creation, per Epoch's page. The earliest dated version on Epoch's page is FrontierMath_10-22-24. Tier 4 development finished June 2025 per the page. The June 12, 2026 date for v2 comes from the Tier 4 v2 benchmark page. Scores are not listed; the 'saturated' claim comes from one news aggregator and is not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: FrontierMath is a set of research-level mathematics problems written by professional mathematicians across most branches of modern maths. Tier 4 is its hardest part, with 43 problems in version 2 (released June 12, 2026). Answers are checked automatically: the model must submit a short Python function that returns the final answer within 30 seconds, and each problem scores 1 or 0.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (2601.21165) and the OpenAI page describe both tracks; "Frontier Science Research" on a release page is the Research track. The two tracks are different tests and are stored as separate benchmarks.
about.what_it_tests: FrontierScience tests expert-level scientific work in two tracks. The Olympiad track holds problems at the level of the international physics, chemistry and biology olympiads with short checkable answers. The Research track holds open-ended, PhD-level sub-problems of real research questions, graded against rubrics by points rather than by a single answer. Release pages print the tracks separately.

about.notes: The GitHub repository was not fetched, and the original launch date is unclear: sources give June 2026 and July 2026 (version 1, 17 tasks). Version 2 was released in September 2026. Model results come from Proximal's own harness, which the team notes is evaluation-aware, and Proximal reports cheating episodes that were zeroed. Independent reproduction is not yet available.
about.what_it_tests: FrontierSWE tests coding agents on very long engineering and research jobs: reimplementing complex systems, speeding up existing code without breaking its correctness, and designing and training machine learning models on held-out data. Version 2 has 34 tasks, each with up to a 20-hour budget per trial. Results are averaged over five trials per task (mean at 5).

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2412.00535 (December 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: FullStackBench tests code generation across the full stack of real programming work: 3,374 problems over 11 domains such as front-end, back-end, data analysis, machine learning and operating systems, in 16 languages, each checked by unit tests in a sandbox. Cards print pass rates on the English and Chinese halves separately.

about.notes: The arXiv page (submitted 13 July 2026, revised 15 July 2026; authors Suhaas Garre, Emily Ritchie, Sushant Mehta, Edwin Chen) gives the item count, the task, the capability tags and the two scores (graded rubric score and strict pass rate). The page does not spell out the exact pass threshold; "all pass rate" on model cards is read as every rubric criterion met. The Surge AI affiliation comes from secondary coverage, not from the arXiv page. The dataset is on Hugging Face.
about.what_it_tests: GDP.pdf tests whether a multimodal model can answer the questions working professionals ask about a specific PDF, such as a lease, a datasheet or a clinical guideline, with the answer grounded in the document. It has 100 items written by professionals in ten fields; an item was kept only if at least two frontier models failed it in a meaningful way. Each item is tagged against eleven capabilities (text extraction and grounding, table and chart comprehension, cross-referencing, spatial reasoning, abstaining on unsupported queries) and scored against a rubric of atomic criteria. Publishers report the strict task-level pass rate ("all pass rate"), the share of items answered well enough to pass every criterion.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (5 October 2025, Tejal Patwardhan and co-authors) describes the task construction and the gold subset. GDPval-AA, the Artificial Analysis re-run reported as an Elo, is the separate family gdpval-aa.
about.what_it_tests: GDPval tests AI models on real deliverables from working professionals: tasks drawn from the work activities of 44 occupations across the nine sectors that contribute most to US GDP, written by people with about 14 years of experience in the job. Expert graders compare the model's deliverable with the human one, and the headline figure is the share of tasks where the model output wins or ties against the professional. A 220-task gold subset is open.

about.maintainer: Artificial Analysis, which runs its own version of OpenAI's GDPval dataset
about.notes: The canonical URL is inferred from the Artificial Analysis evaluation URL pattern and the search result; the methodology page returned 404 when fetched. The launch year was not stated in the sources read. BenchLM reports a different normalized-percentage metric, and the Elo leaderboard figures were not verified on the primary site.
about.what_it_tests: GDPval-AA is Artificial Analysis's version of OpenAI's GDPval, a set of realistic work tasks drawn from 44 occupations in nine major industries. Models get shell access and web browsing in an agent loop and produce a work product, and the outputs are compared in blind pairwise judgments that are turned into Elo ratings. The v2 revision re-anchors the scale so that human-expert deliverables sit near 1000 points.

about.notes: The relation to GeneBench Pro (family genebench-pro) is inferred from the names; the page does not state it. Values under the two names are kept apart.
about.what_it_tests: GeneBench is printed on the GPT-5.5 release page among the academic evaluations with a pass rate per model and no further description. The later GPT-5.6 page reports GeneBench Pro, a computational biology benchmark OpenAI published separately, so GeneBench is read as its predecessor or base version.

about.notes: The OpenAI page returned HTTP 403 when read, so the facts come from secondary coverage that agrees on a June 30, 2026 release and the 129-problem count. One outlet describes it as 10 genomics case studies, which conflicts with the count. Ten questions were said to be open-sourced on Hugging Face; not verified.
about.what_it_tests: GeneBench-Pro tests AI agents on computational biology work where no single method is obviously right. It contains 129 problems across 10 domains and 21 subdomains, including statistical genetics, cancer genomics, clinical diagnostics and pharmacogenomics. OpenAI describes it as measuring judgement about analysis choices rather than factual recall, and grading is deterministic.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2412.03304 (December 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: Global-MMLU is a multilingual version of MMLU with professionally and community translated questions in 42 languages, annotated for cultural sensitivity. Global-MMLU-Lite is the smaller balanced subset. The score is accuracy averaged over the languages reported.

about.maintainer: Tyler A. Chang, Catherine Arnett and co-authors with the MRL 2025 shared task participants
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2510.24081 (October 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: Global PIQA is a participatory physical commonsense reasoning benchmark: physical-intuition questions in the PIQA style written by native speakers for over 100 languages, with culturally local content rather than translations. The score is accuracy averaged over the languages.

about.maintainer: David Rein and co-authors (NYU, Cohere, Anthropic)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2311.12022 (November 2023). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: GPQA is a set of 448 graduate-level multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry written and validated by domain experts so that skilled non-experts with web access still fail most of them. The main set is reported here when a card prints "GPQA" without a subset; the Diamond subset is catalogued separately.

about.maintainer: David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland, Jackson Petty, Richard Yuanzhe Pang, Julien Dirani, Julian Michael and Samuel R. Bowman
