Aggregators disagree: LLM Stats lists one self-reported model, while BenchmarkList lists five models with a top score of 63.1 percent, dated 2026-08-03, which was not verified. No paper or methodology was found.
about.what_it_tests: QwenQoderBench is an in-house Qwen benchmark for coding agents, which the Qwen3.8 model card describes as an inhouse benchmark for evaluating user experience on Qoder. The card reports results from Qwen's own testing, and the 2.4T flagship card lists a score of 58.4. The benchmark measures coding-agent tasks, and BenchmarkList reports it as Avg@5.

about.notes: Written from footnote 12 of the Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B model page, which is Alibaba Qwen's own page. The footnote says the benchmark uses Claude Code as its harness (a third-party coding agent), which is recorded here because it affects the result. No paper or release date was found, so introduced is null. Aggregators (BenchLM, LLM Stats) disagree on scores; none are used.
about.what_it_tests: QwenReactBench is an in-house Qwen benchmark of building React web projects, bilingual in English and Chinese, across seven categories. The model builds a project, the project is rendered automatically, and a multimodal judge grades the result. Results are ranked with a Bradley-Terry Elo-style rating, and the page does not state the number of tasks.

about.notes: Written from footnote 13 of the Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B model page, Alibaba Qwen's own page. No separate paper or release date was found, so introduced is null. Aggregators name the benchmark only as QwenSVG and their scores are not used. A separate public SVG leaderboard (Design Arena) is a different benchmark.
about.what_it_tests: QwenSVGBench is an in-house Qwen benchmark of SVG code generation, where the model writes SVG vector graphics from a prompt. It is bilingual in English and Chinese, the output is rendered automatically, and a multimodal judge grades it. Results are ranked with a Bradley-Terry Elo-style rating, and the page does not state the number of prompts.

about.notes: Versions differ: the 2.4T card gives 80.7, while AI Release Tracker lists Qwen3.8-27B at 79 and a QwenSWEBench V2 row appears in the Max-0902 table. Harnesses differ across comparisons, so the scores are not directly comparable. The task-level description is from secondary sources rather than the card.
about.what_it_tests: QwenSWEBench is Qwen's in-house software-engineering benchmark: it tests repository-level issue resolution, meaning fixing real problems in software projects. Scores are self-reported by Qwen. A later Qwen3.8-Max-0902 comparison lists a QwenSWEBench V2 score of 70.0 under a different harness.

about.notes: Described only in the notes under the Language table of the Qwen3.6 model cards; the task set and the judge are not public.
about.what_it_tests: QwenWebBench is an in-house front-end code generation benchmark of the Qwen team: bilingual (English and Chinese) prompts in seven categories, web design, web apps, games, SVG, data visualization, animation and 3D. Outputs are rendered automatically and judged by a multimodal model on code and visual correctness; models are ranked against each other with a Bradley-Terry / Elo rating, so the printed number is a rating, not a percentage.

about.notes: The Hugging Face dataset card (fetched, undated) gives the 765-row test split, the image and question format and the CC BY-ND 4.0 licence. The xAI announcement page (https://x.ai/news/grok-1.5v, dated 12 April 2024) introduces RealWorldQA as a benchmark for basic real-world spatial understanding and gives the release date; neither page describes a scoring method.
about.what_it_tests: RealWorldQA tests basic real-world spatial understanding in multimodal models. The test split has 765 rows, each pairing one image with one question and a short answer; the initial release has over 700 images, some taken from vehicles and others from real-world photos. Questions cover items such as traffic lights, lane layout, object counts, relative position and size. Most questions are multiple choice and the rest are open-ended, with a single word or number as the answer; the dataset card does not describe how answers are scored.

about.notes: The only public description is the note under the VL Performance table of the Qwen3.8-27B model card (August 2026). The task set, the scoring rule and the version history are not public, so values cannot be reproduced outside the Qwen team.
about.what_it_tests: RecreationBench is an in-house, long-horizon benchmark of the Qwen team in which an agent recreates an application, exercising hybrid-agent capabilities across five platforms: desktop (Ubuntu, macOS and Windows), mobile (Android) and the web. The card prints one number per model and does not name the metric or the task count.

about.maintainer: Licheng Yu, Sahar Kazemzadeh and co-authors (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and others); COCO images
about.notes: The RefCOCO and RefCOCO+ splits date from Kazemzadeh et al. 2014 and Yu et al. 2016, RefCOCOg from Mao et al. 2016. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg are referring-expression grounding sets on COCO images: given a phrase such as "the man in the red shirt on the left", the model must return the bounding box of that object. A prediction counts when its box overlaps the reference box by at least 0.5 IoU; model cards print an average accuracy over the splits of the three sets.

about.maintainer: Enshen Zhou and co-authors (the RoboRefer work, Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence and Peking University)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2506.04308 (June 2025, RoboRefer). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: RefSpatial-Bench tests spatial referring for robotics: the model must point to a location in an image described in words, such as a spot to the left of one object and behind another, in two tasks, Location and Placement, with multi-step reasoning. A prediction counts when the point falls inside the ground-truth mask; the score is accuracy.

about.notes: The Reka announcement (28 August 2025) describes the question set and the checklist judge. xAI prints it as "Research-Eval Reka" with a bare score.
about.what_it_tests: Research-Eval tests search-augmented models on 374 questions that need information from different kinds of websites, chosen to be closer to everyday research questions than puzzle-style deep-research sets. Each question comes with a checklist of requirements, and an LLM judge scores an answer against that checklist.

about.maintainer: ResearchRubrics authors (lead author Manasi Sharma); the maintaining organisation is not named on the arXiv page
about.notes: The arXiv abstract page (submitted 10 November 2025, Manasi Sharma listed first of 16 authors) gives the 2,500+ rubrics and the under-68% compliance result. It does not give the prompt count, the domain count, or how rubric weights and grading work; secondary summaries give conflicting figures (101 prompts, 9 or 10 domains), so they are not used here. No benchmark site or repository was opened, and the model-card label carries no version on this page.
about.what_it_tests: ResearchRubrics tests whether a deep research agent can answer open-ended research prompts that are judged against expert-written rubrics. The benchmark contains realistic, domain-diverse prompts and more than 2,500 fine-grained expert-written rubrics. The reported result is average rubric compliance: the paper's abstract reports that the leading deep research systems reach under 68% average compliance.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: authors Suhaas Garre, Erik Knutsen, Sushant Mehta and Edwin Chen; the release is described by Surge HQ. The catalog attribution to Google is not supported: neither Google nor DeepMind appears on the arXiv page. The paper is listed as accepted to ICLR 2026 and revised June 23, 2026. The problem count is not on the page; a search result mentions 25 problems under the alias RMBench. Surge attribution comes from the authors and a Surge HQ blog seen in search results.
about.what_it_tests: RiemannBench tests research-level mathematics that goes well beyond olympiad-style problems. It is a private set of expert-written problems, each with a unique closed-form answer that is checked by a program, and each problem is verified by two experts solving it independently. Models run as unconstrained research agents with coding tools and search, and are scored with a statistical estimator over many independent runs.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2404.06654 (April 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: RULER is a synthetic long-context benchmark: needle-in-a-haystack retrieval with several needles, multi-hop tracing, aggregation and question answering over padded contexts of fixed lengths (4K to 1M tokens and beyond). The score at a given length is accuracy over the tasks; "RULER-100" denotes the 100-task set evaluated at the stated context length.

about.maintainer: UniPat-AI (GitHub owner of the official repository); the arXiv paper's lead author is Kean Shi
about.notes: The arXiv abstract page (submitted 15 May 2026, Kean Shi and 15 co-authors) and the GitHub README give the 23 systems, 106 tasks and six domains. The two primary pages disagree in emphasis: the arXiv page says the strongest model completes fewer than 4% of tasks end-to-end, while a secondary search summary cites a checkpoint score near 44%, so no headline percentage is stated here. Do not confuse it with SaaSBench (arXiv 2605.17526), a separate 30-task coding benchmark.
about.what_it_tests: SaaS-Bench tests whether a computer-use agent can complete professional workflows by operating real, self-hosted SaaS applications through a browser. The benchmark has 106 tasks across 23 SaaS systems in six domains (business, healthcare, software, teamwork, agriculture and media), split into a text-only track and a multimodal track. Each task is a multi-step business workflow, and a per-task verifier reads the running application's database, API and page state, plus LLM-judged content checks, to give weighted checkpoint scores with partial credit. The paper also reports strict end-to-end task completion, which is much lower.

about.notes: The arXiv abstract page (submitted 18 July 2024, first author Minyang Tian, 30 authors in total) gives the 80 main problems, the 338 subproblems, the 16 subfields and the percentage-solved metric. It does not describe the scoring procedure beyond the gold-standard tests, and it reflects the 2024 paper only; later revisions or leaderboard numbers were not checked.
about.what_it_tests: SciCode tests whether language models can write code that solves real research problems in the natural sciences. The benchmark has 80 main problems split into 338 subproblems, each combining knowledge recall, reasoning and code synthesis, across 16 natural-science subfields including mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and materials science. The problems were curated with scientists, and scientist-annotated gold-standard solutions and test cases are used for evaluation. The metric is the percentage of problems solved, and the best model tested in the paper's most realistic setting solved 4.6% of problems.

about.maintainer: Kaixin Li, Ziyang Meng, Hongzhan Lin, Ziyang Luo, Yuchen Tian, Jing Ma, Zhiyong Huang and Tat-Seng Chua
about.notes: Maintainer detail: affiliations not on the arXiv page; the ACM Multimedia 2025 version is listed by HKBU. arXiv v1 April 4, 2025. The arXiv page does not describe the scoring rule; the point-in-box rule comes from a secondary listing (alphaXiv). The 'no tools' label is a catalog variant and was not checked against a primary source.
about.what_it_tests: ScreenSpot-Pro tests whether a multimodal AI model can find the right spot on a screen. Each item gives a high-resolution screenshot of professional software, across 23 applications in five industries and three operating systems, plus a written instruction, and the model must point to the matching element. A prediction counts as correct if its predicted point falls inside the target element's bounding box.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2410.23218 (October 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: ScreenSpot-v2 is the corrected version of ScreenSpot: given a screenshot of a desktop, mobile or web interface and an instruction, the model has to locate the target element. The score is grounding accuracy.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2506.01062 (June 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: Seal-0 is the core subset of SealQA, a benchmark of search-augmented question answering whose questions bring back conflicting, noisy or unhelpful web results. Seal-0 keeps the questions on which frontier models with search mostly failed when the set was built, so it measures whether a model can reason over contradictory evidence instead of trusting the first result. The score is accuracy.

about.maintainer: Hwiwon Lee, Jiawei Liu, Dongjun Kim, Wubing Xia, Ziqi Zhang, Chunqiu Steven Xia and Lingming Zhang
about.notes: Maintainer detail: authors; affiliations not shown on the arXiv page. Printed label says OpenAI, which is not the paper's maintainer; the authors are academic. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists SEC-Bench Pro among OpenAI's cyber evaluations. Aggregator leaderboards disagree on the top score, so no score is given. The paper is a follow-up to the earlier SEC-bench (NeurIPS 2025). v1 was posted 2026-05-26 and v2 revised 2026-07-20.
about.what_it_tests: SEC-bench Pro tests whether AI coding agents can find real, previously disclosed security bugs in large, critical software, mainly the V8 and SpiderMonkey JavaScript engines. It contains 183 validated cases, each packaged in a container with a fixed version and a checkable crash result. The agents work without hints such as sanitizer output that names the vulnerable function, and the authors use an LLM judge to grade results.

about.notes: Written as remembered; the repository was not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: SecCodeBench tests whether code written by a model is secure: coding tasks where a working but vulnerable solution is easy, scored by whether the output both works and avoids the vulnerability. The score is the share of tasks solved securely.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (7 November 2024) describes the grading. Values printed under an "agentic" or "with search" heading were obtained with search tools and are a different setting from the closed-book one.
about.what_it_tests: SimpleQA tests short-form factual recall with questions collected to be hard for GPT-4. Each answer is graded correct, incorrect or not attempted, and publishers print the share graded correct.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (9 September 2025) describes the cleaning and the grader.
about.what_it_tests: SimpleQA Verified is a cleaned 1,000-question version of SimpleQA, with mislabeled answers, duplicates and topic imbalance fixed. An automated grader marks each answer, and the paper reports an F1 score; model cards usually print accuracy or pass@1.

about.notes: Written from the arXiv listing as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: SimpleVQA tests the factual knowledge of multimodal models with short-answer questions about what an image shows, in the spirit of SimpleQA for text: the questions are objective, the answers are short and checked for correctness, so the score is the share of questions answered correctly rather than a reasoning rate.

about.maintainer: Academic author team led by Xiangyi Li
about.notes: Maintainer detail: with Wenbo Chen, Yimin Liu, Shenghan Zheng, Han-chung Lee and others (about 42 authors; affiliations not confirmed. Posted to arXiv 2026-02-13; built on the Harbor framework. Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. Arcade.dev's 'SkillBench' is a different project (a scoring index of skills) and is not this benchmark.
about.what_it_tests: SkillsBench tests whether reusable instruction packages, called skills, actually help AI agents on real tasks. It has about 84 to 86 tasks across 11 domains (sources differ on the count), each with an automatic checker that decides pass or fail. Each task is run with no skills, with curated skills, and with skills the model wrote itself; curated skills raised average pass rates by about 16 percentage points, while self-written skills gave no average gain.

about.maintainer: Bo Liu and co-authors (Hong Kong Polytechnic University and others)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2102.09542 (ISBI 2021). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: SLAKE is a bilingual (English and Chinese) medical visual question answering set of 642 radiology images with about 14,000 questions, with semantic annotations and a medical knowledge base behind them. Cards usually print overall accuracy on the English test split.

about.maintainer: RUCKBReasoning (GitHub owner of the official repository); the arXiv abstract page names the authors, led by Zeyao Ma
about.notes: The arXiv abstract page (submitted 21 June 2024, lead author Zeyao Ma with eight co-authors, v2 revised 17 October 2024) and the GitHub README (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks, spotlight) confirm 912 instructions and 2,729 test cases. The README does not mention a SpreadsheetBench 2; the nearest item it names is SpreadsheetBench Verified (400 instances, announced 2025/12), so the model-card label SpreadsheetBench 2 is unverified and may refer to a different release. The README gives no leaderboard figure, so no score is stated here.
about.what_it_tests: SpreadsheetBench tests whether an AI model can carry out real-world spreadsheet manipulation. The 912 instructions were collected from online Excel forums and cover spreadsheets with multiple tables, non-standard relational tables and non-textual elements. Each instruction has several spreadsheet files as test cases, 2,729 in total (about three per instruction), and outputs are judged in an online-judge style, with formulas recalculated before the check. The dataset is released under CC BY-SA 4.0.

about.maintainer: Vals AI publishes and hosts the benchmark page
about.notes: Maintainer detail: DAPLab at Columbia University lists it as its project; paper authors Jeremy Spence, Nicholas Assaderaghi, Jinhao Zhu, Nikil Ravi and others. Printed label says OpenAI, and the name is misleading: 'SRE' here does not mean site reliability engineering. The Vals AI page and the DAPLab page both claim it, and the paper (arXiv 2608.11469, first posted 2026-08-11, revised 2026-10-01) lists its authors without a single institution, so the maintainer is given as both. The DAPLab page marks it 'In progress'. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists SRE-Bench as an OpenAI evaluation with pass@1 and pass@4 scores; the card's figures are not quoted here.
about.what_it_tests: SRE-Bench is a reverse-engineering benchmark, not a site-reliability one: it tests whether AI agents can work out what a compiled program does when no source code is given. Agents use a shell sandbox with standard analysis tools across five areas (network protocols, firmware, games, file-format recovery and malware). The benchmark has 262 binaries and 1,572 tasks that are graded deterministically.

about.maintainer: Alexandra Souly, Qingyuan Lu and co-authors (UC Berkeley)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2402.10260 (February 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: StrongREJECT scores how well a model resists jailbreak attempts: forbidden prompts are wrapped in known jailbreak techniques and a rubric-based judge rates whether the reply is a harmful, specific and convincing answer. Model cards print the share of attempts refused, so higher is better.

about.maintainer: Shuran Song, Samuel Lichtenberg and Jianxiong Xiao (Princeton University)
about.notes: Dataset paper CVPR 2015. The task and metric behind the Qwen cell are not stated on the card; written as remembered, not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: SUN RGB-D is a benchmark of about 10,000 RGB-D indoor images with 2D and 3D object bounding boxes and room layouts, used for 3D object detection and scene understanding. Multimodal model cards use it to score 3D grounding; the Qwen cards print a single number without naming the metric.

about.maintainer: M-A-P team and ByteDance (Xinrun Du and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (20 February 2025) describes the disciplines and the filtering.
about.what_it_tests: SuperGPQA tests graduate-level knowledge and reasoning across 285 disciplines, including applied fields that other benchmarks leave out, with questions filtered by experts and models. The score is accuracy.

about.notes: Known only from the Mistral Large 4 release page (October 2026). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: A blind human evaluation of coding quality run by Surge AI for Mistral AI: professional annotators rate model outputs on a 1 to 5 scale with model identities hidden. The score is the mean rating.

families.name: Surge AI Human Eval on Code

about.notes: Named on the IFM K2-Horizon model card (September 2026). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-Atlas-QnA asks repository-level questions about real codebases that an agent has to answer by exploring the code; the strict setting runs without internet access. The score is the share of questions answered correctly. Sister tasks cover refactoring and test writing.

about.maintainer: SWE-bench team (Kabir Khandpur, Kilian Lieret, Carlos E. Jimenez, Ofir Press, John Yang)
about.notes: The SWE-bench site describes the tasks and the scoring; it cites the 2025 SWE-smith paper.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-bench Multilingual tests agentic software engineering outside Python: 300 issue-fixing tasks from 42 repositories in nine languages (C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, PHP, Ruby, Rust). A task is solved when the agent's patch makes the failing tests pass without breaking the passing ones; the score is the share of tasks resolved.

about.notes: Scale Labs published it on September 19, 2025. The original launch figures (top models below 25 percent) reflect 2025 models and are far below current third-party leaderboard figures. The paper's authors are listed under Scale Labs. The 'printed by Google, Alibaba' labels were not checked against model cards.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-Bench Pro tests AI agents on realistic, long-horizon software engineering tasks in real codebases, often requiring multi-file patches that a professional engineer might take hours or days to finish. It has 1,865 problems from 41 actively maintained repositories, split into a public set, a held-out set and a commercial set from startup partners. Results are reported as Pass@1 under a unified scaffold, and a patch counts only if it passes the verifying tests.

about.maintainer: OpenAI (built on SWE-bench by Princeton University)
about.notes: SWE-bench itself is the Princeton benchmark of arXiv 2310.06770 (October 2023); the Verified subset was released by OpenAI in August 2024 with the annotation process described on its page. Publishers differ in the subset they run (all 500 problems, or a fixed subset that works on their infrastructure) and in the agent harness; the pass rate is a percentage of the problems attempted.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated subset of 500 tasks from SWE-bench, the benchmark where a model receives a real GitHub issue from a Python repository and must produce a patch that makes the hidden tests pass. Professional software developers screened the original tasks and kept those with a clear problem statement and fair tests, so a failure reflects the model rather than a broken task.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (February 2025, Samuel Miserendino and co-authors) describes the task set and the Diamond subset. "IC Diamond" on a release page is the individual contributor part of the public subset, scored as a pass rate here rather than as dollars earned.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-Lancer tests whether a model can earn money doing real freelance software engineering. Its tasks are more than 1,400 jobs posted on Upwork for the Expensify codebase, worth one million US dollars in payouts together, from small bug fixes to feature builds. Individual contributor (IC) tasks are graded by end-to-end tests written by professional engineers; manager tasks ask the model to pick the best of several proposals. The public subset is called Diamond.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (first author Rishi Desai; affiliations not shown on the NeurIPS page); the xAI attribution rests on a third-party review of Grok 4.5 launch numbers. The xAI 29.0 percent pass@1 figure for Grok 4.5 comes from a third-party review page, not an xAI primary source, and was not verified. An AI Engineer talk reported a historical best of 26 percent. The paper reports that about 18.8 percent of rollouts showed reward hacking. The NeurIPS 2026 poster page gives no author affiliations, so the xAI link is unconfirmed.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-Marathon tests whether AI agents can autonomously complete ultra-long software work. It has 20 long-horizon tasks across software engineering and adjacent technical fields, each with a unique executable environment, a human-written reference solution and a multi-layer verification suite. A task counts as resolved when the verifier accepts the agent's work, and the paper says frontier coding agents resolve fewer than 20 percent of tasks.

about.maintainer: SWE-bench team (first author John Yang), per the arXiv listing
about.notes: The arXiv paper (submitted 4 October 2024, first author John Yang, cs.CL) is the closest primary source found for a multimodal software engineering benchmark with images in issues. Neither the abstract nor the full text uses the name SWE-MM; the label comes from the Qwen3.8-27B model card, whose note says SWE-MM is scored on the public dev split of SWE-bench Multimodal with modifications taken from an Anthropic system card, so a card value rests on that split, not the full set. The abstract gives 617 instances while the body gives 619.
about.what_it_tests: SWE-bench Multimodal, which the paper abbreviates as SWE-bench M, tests whether an autonomous software engineering system can fix bugs in visual, user-facing JavaScript software. Each task instance includes at least one image in its problem statement or unit tests. The paper reports 617 task instances in its abstract and 619 in its body and conclusion, drawn from 17 JavaScript libraries used for web interface design, diagramming, data visualization, syntax highlighting and interactive mapping. A task instance counts as resolved when all unit tests pass, and the main metric is the percentage of resolved instances.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (17 June 2024) describes the state-based scoring. tau2-bench is the separate successor with a telecom domain.
about.what_it_tests: tau-bench tests an agent that talks to a simulated user while using domain tools under policy rules, in an airline and a retail domain. A run passes when the final database state matches the annotated target; the score is the pass rate, with pass^k for repeated trials.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (9 June 2025, Victor Barres and co-authors) describes the dual-control design. Publishers differ on prompt adjustments: the GPT-5.5 page reports its own models with the original prompts and omits other labs for that reason.
about.what_it_tests: tau2-bench tests a customer service agent in a conversation where both sides act: the agent and a simulated user each have tools that change a shared environment, so the agent must reason about the state and guide the user through steps the user alone can perform. The telecom domain (troubleshooting a phone line) is the dual-control setting; tasks are built from verifiable atomic components and a task passes when the final state matches the expected one.

about.notes: The repository README (which presents the project as tau3-bench) gives the release description, the banking_knowledge domain, the July 2026 fix and the install extra, but does not state the task count or the launch date. The 97-question count, the pass@1 metric and the backend-state grading come from the Artificial Analysis methodology page, which lists the domain under 'Legacy Evaluations' as tau3-Banking; the naming and version may differ from the current repository. The year 2026 is taken from the companion tau-Knowledge paper (arXiv:2603.04370), which the README dates only to 2026.
about.what_it_tests: tau3-Banking is the banking_knowledge domain of Sierra's tau3-bench (tau-cubed), a knowledge-retrieval customer-service benchmark. The agent serves a bank customer in a simulated agent-user conversation and has to find answers in banking policy and product documents, using the retrieval setup it is given: configurable RAG pipelines, document search, embeddings or agentic shell-based search. Artificial Analysis lists the evaluation as 'Dual control agent-user simulation with knowledge retrieval', with 97 questions, 5 repeats and a pass@1 metric, and scores it by backend database state evaluation. The domain was corrected in the v1.0.1 release of July 2026, which fixed a couple of banking_knowledge task errors.

about.notes: The tau2-bench repository presents the project as tau3-bench; see the separate tau3-Banking family for the banking_knowledge domain. The GLM-5.1 card prints one number labelled tau3-Bench without a domain.
about.what_it_tests: tau3-bench (tau-cubed) is the third generation of the Sierra tau-bench line of customer-service agent tests: the agent talks to a simulated user and acts through domain tools under policy rules, and the new generation adds knowledge-retrieval and voice domains. A run passes when the final state matches the annotated target; the score is the pass rate. Model cards that print a single tau3-bench number do not say which domains are averaged.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: run through the Harbor framework. Project leads named in the repository README: Ryan Marten, Alex Shaw, Andy Konwinski, Ludwig Schmidt. Maintainers and sandboxed-container design come from the GitHub README. The May 19, 2025 launch date comes from a tbench.ai page seen only in search snippets. The Version 2.0 facts (89 tasks, November 7, 2025) come from secondary coverage. The README does not describe scoring; the leaderboard is on Harbor Hub.
about.what_it_tests: Terminal-Bench tests whether an AI agent can finish real jobs by typing commands into a Linux terminal, such as building software, configuring a system or processing files. Each task runs in its own sandboxed container, and the agent succeeds only if the final state of that container passes the task's automatic checks. Version 2.0 (November 2025) has 89 hand-checked tasks, and the companion Harbor framework runs the agents.

about.maintainer: Terminal-Bench-Science team, led by researchers at Stanford University, built with the Terminal-Bench and Harbor team
about.notes: The citation dates v0.1.0 to August 2026 and the page gives no exact release date. The page does not report a cost-per-task metric; it reports total cost across the 70 tasks, so the catalog's average-cost label is not supported. Top-model results conflict between tbench.ai (30%) and Snorkel pages (40%), so no score is given.
about.what_it_tests: Terminal-Bench-Science tests AI agents on the computational workflows working scientists actually run, not textbook questions. Each task is a containerised terminal job, such as statistical analysis, simulation, signal processing or proofs, and the output is checked by task-specific automated tests. Version 0.1 has 70 tasks written by practising researchers across life, physical, Earth, mathematical and engineering sciences.

about.notes: Written from the arXiv listing (November 2025) as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: TIR-Bench tests "thinking with images": visual reasoning tasks that need the model to act on the picture, zoom, crop, rotate, draw or run code over it, rather than answer from a single look. The score is accuracy; cards print it with and without a code interpreter.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Junlong Li, Junxian He and co-authors), with collaborators at All Hands AI, Carnegie Mellon and Duke. Accepted to ICLR 2026; code at github.com/hkust-nlp/toolathlon. The paper's first version names a different top model than a later version, so leaderboard leaders depend on the version cited. Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. The 'Verified (Pass@1)' label refers to a subset or setting that was not checked in this run.
about.what_it_tests: Toolathlon (The Tool Decathlon) tests whether language agents can finish long, realistic workflows across many software applications. It covers 32 applications and 604 tools, from calendars and notes to databases and cloud consoles, with 108 tasks that take about 20 turns on average. Each task has its own automatic check of the final state, and the environments run in isolated containers.

about.maintainer: University of Washington (Mandar Joshi and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (9 May 2017) describes the question collection. The setting a card used (with or without evidence documents) is stored with the observation when stated.
about.what_it_tests: TriviaQA tests reading comprehension and recall with about 95,000 trivia questions written by enthusiasts, each paired with evidence documents. Model cards usually print exact-match accuracy on the answers, often without the evidence documents, which turns it into a knowledge test.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2003.05002 (March 2020). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: TyDi QA is a question-answering benchmark over 11 typologically diverse languages with questions written by native speakers without seeing the answer passage. The score is F1 averaged over languages.

about.maintainer: Penghao Wu and Saining Xie (New York University)
about.notes: Written from the paper "V*: Guided Visual Search as a Core Mechanism in Multimodal LLMs" (December 2023) as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: V* Bench tests whether a multimodal model can find and reason about small visual details in high-resolution images: 191 images with questions about the attributes of a small object or the spatial relation between two of them, where the answer is only visible after locating the right region. The score is accuracy over the multiple-choice questions.

about.notes: The Vals page gives version history from v1 to v2.1 (v2 on August 13, 2026; v2.1 on September 25, 2026) but not the original introduction date. Third-party mirrors (BenchLM, capitalandcompute) show earlier versions with different scores and leaders, which are not comparable.
about.what_it_tests: The Vals Index is a single composite score from Vals AI that averages agentic tasks in finance, coding, legal and tax work. Each sector is weighted by its share of US GDP, with finance carrying the most weight, and each sector score is the average of its benchmarks. The current version, 2.1, combines Finance Agent v2 and an Excel modeling benchmark for finance, Terminal-Bench 4.0, Vibe Code Bench and a code migration task for coding, and legal and tax benchmarks.

about.notes: Description written from the Andon Labs evaluation page as remembered; the page was not re-read for this record. Z.ai model cards state that the runs are conducted independently by Andon Labs.
about.what_it_tests: Vending-Bench puts a model in charge of a simulated vending-machine business for a long run of simulated days: it orders stock from suppliers by e-mail, sets prices, pays fees and keeps the machine filled, using tools in a long multi-turn loop. The result is the money in the bank at the end of the run, so the unit is dollars rather than a percentage. Version 2 is the harder successor with a stricter simulation and a fixed one-year horizon.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with paper authors Hung Tran, Langston Nashold, Rayan Krishnan, Antoine Bigeard and Alex Gu. Paper submitted March 4, 2026 (v3 May 13, 2026), accepted to ACM CAIS 2026. The best test-split result of 61.8% was reported in the paper; leaderboard figures for later v1.1 and 1-100 variants come from aggregators and are not repeated here. A search snippet linked MIT researchers to the paper, which the arXiv page did not confirm.
about.what_it_tests: Vibe Code Bench tests whether an AI model can build a complete, working web application from a written description, starting from nothing. The benchmark has 100 app specifications split into validation and held-out test sets. An automated browser agent then checks each deployed app against 964 multi-step user workflows, and the score is the accuracy across their 10,131 steps.

about.maintainer: Chaoyou Fu (lead author) and co-authors; code and data under the MME-Benchmarks GitHub organization
about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 31 May 2024, lead author Chaoyou Fu, latest revision dated 30 May 2025) gives the video count, the 254 hours, the question count and the human annotation. The abstract does not say how accuracy is computed; the GitHub README (video-mme.github.io links to it) gives the subtitle rule and a 2024.06.15 refresh of the evaluation, so the version and the subtitle setting matter. The 'w. sub' label on model cards is the publisher's setting.
about.what_it_tests: Video-MME tests whether a multimodal model can analyze video content across a wide range of clip lengths. The set holds 900 videos totaling 254 hours, with durations from 11 seconds to 1 hour, and 2,700 question-answer pairs. All data was newly collected and annotated by humans rather than taken from an existing video dataset. Model cards print Video-MME (w. sub), the setting in which the model also receives the subtitles matched to the sampled video frames; the score is accuracy, broken down by video duration, domain, subcategory and task type.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (January 2025, Kairui Hu and co-authors) describes the three-stage design. Release pages print it as "Video MMMU" or "VideoMMMU"; "no tools" on a release page is the publisher's setup note.
about.what_it_tests: Video-MMMU tests whether a multimodal model can learn from videos. It holds 300 expert-level lecture videos across six disciplines with 900 questions arranged in three stages of knowledge acquisition: perception (reading what is shown), comprehension (understanding the concept) and adaptation (applying it to a new problem). Accuracy on the questions is the score.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with the Center for AI Safety; lead authors include Jasper Gotting and Pedro Medeiros, with Seth Donoughe as corresponding author. A SecureBio newsletter describes a 350-question version, which differs from the 322 in the paper; the arXiv v2 is used here. Model scores come from a 2025 paper and are dated.
about.what_it_tests: The Virology Capabilities Test is a set of 322 multimodal questions, written with dozens of PhD-level virologists, about troubleshooting complex virology lab protocols. The questions cover factual, tacit and image-based knowledge, and models are scored by accuracy. In the April 2025 paper, expert virologists averaged about 22 percent on questions in their own sub-areas, and the best model listed there scored about 44 percent.

about.maintainer: zai-org (GitHub organisation); paper first author Zehai He with co-authors
about.notes: The arXiv abstract (arXiv 2603.26648, first submitted 27 March 2026, first author Zehai He) gives the 193 tasks, 918 prototype images, 1,255 test cases, the three levels and the agent-verification paradigm. The README gives the per-level task counts and the scoring split, and it states a CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 licence that limits use to non-commercial research. The arXiv abstract was revised as v3 on 20 July 2026, so the catalog should name the version it cites.
about.what_it_tests: Vision2Web tests whether a multimodal coding agent can turn visual prototypes and text specifications into working websites. The benchmark has 193 tasks across 16 subcategories in four domains (e-commerce, SaaS, content and public service), with 918 prototype images and 1,255 functional test cases. Tasks fall into three levels: static webpages (100 tasks), interactive multi-page frontends (66 tasks) and full-stack websites (27 tasks). Level 1 is scored by a Visual Score, and levels 2 and 3 add a Functional Score, with GUI agent verifiers checking functional correctness and a VLM-based judge comparing prototypes with screenshots.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2509.26490 (September 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry. The Qwen3.6 cards judge with Claude 4 Sonnet because the official judge is no longer available.
about.what_it_tests: VitaBench tests agents on versatile interactive tasks from daily life, such as food delivery, in-store services and travel, with simulated users, tools and policies, including cross-scenario tasks that combine them. A judge scores whether the task was completed; cards print an average over the sub-domains.

about.maintainer: Pooyan Rahmanzadehgervi and co-authors (Auburn University and University of Alberta)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2407.06581 (July 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: VLMs are Blind (BlindTest) is a set of seven very simple visual tasks that people solve at a glance, such as whether two lines intersect, whether two circles overlap, which letter is circled, and counting nested squares or grid rows. It measures low-level visual perception rather than knowledge; the score is average accuracy over the tasks.

about.maintainer: Yiming Chen and co-authors (National University of Singapore)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2410.17196 (October 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: VoiceBench evaluates speech-input assistants on spoken versions of instruction, knowledge and safety tests under varied speakers, environments and content conditions. The score is the average over its sub-tests.

about.maintainer: Runqi Qiao and co-authors (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications and others)
about.notes: Paper arXiv 2407.01284 (July 2024). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: We-Math tests visual mathematical reasoning by breaking each problem into the knowledge concepts it needs, so that a model can be scored not only on the final answer but on whether it has the sub-steps right. It has 6,500 problems over 67 concepts; cards print one accuracy, usually the strict score on the test set.

about.maintainer: Shuyan Zhou et al. (original WebArena paper); ServiceNow (WebArena-Verified release)
about.notes: The ServiceNow README (fetched) calls WebArena-Verified the verified release of WebArena and gives the 812-task set, the 258-task Hard subset, the removal of LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and dated announcements up to 2 February 2026. The arXiv abstract (submitted 25 July 2023, lead author Shuyan Zhou) describes the original environment and its four domains but does not mention a verified release. The README gives no version number and does not say whether the 812 set has changed since release; a workshop paper on the Verified release was seen only as a search snippet giving a 137-task Hard subset, so the 258 figure should be confirmed against the repository.
about.what_it_tests: WebArena tests whether a language-guided agent can complete tasks on realistic, self-hosted websites. The environment provides functional sites in four domains: e-commerce, social forums, collaborative software development and content management, plus tools such as a map and external knowledge sources. WebArena-Verified is the corrected release of the task set: the full set has 812 verified tasks and the Hard subset has 258 tasks. Its evaluators are deterministic and run offline on network trace replay, with LLM-as-a-judge evaluation removed.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: co-first and corresponding authors listed on the arXiv paper. arXiv 2508.07999 (August 2025). Project page widesearch-seed.github.io; dataset and code are on Hugging Face and GitHub under ByteDance-Seed. Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms.
about.what_it_tests: WideSearch tests whether AI search agents can gather a large amount of information completely and accurately, such as a full table of facts about many entities, rather than a single answer. It has 200 questions in English and Chinese across more than 15 domains, drawn from real user queries, and each asks for many facts that are checked one at a time. The main score is an exact match to the reference table, and most systems scored close to zero while the best scored about 5 percent.

about.notes: Named on the IFM K2-Horizon model card (September 2026); the card uses a subset of English text-only tasks. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: WildClawBench collects in-the-wild agentic tasks of the kind users give autonomous assistants, with text-only and multimodal subsets; a task passes when its checker accepts the final result. The score is the pass rate on the subset the publisher states.

about.maintainer: Allen Institute for AI (Keisuke Sakaguchi and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (24 July 2019) describes the construction and the bias reduction.
about.what_it_tests: WinoGrande tests commonsense reasoning with 44,000 pronoun-resolution problems in the style of the Winograd Schema Challenge, built at scale and filtered to remove shortcuts. The score is the share of problems answered correctly.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with Scale AI and a group of academic and technical partners; authors include Nathaniel Li, Alexander Pan and Dan Hendrycks. The number of questions differs by version: the early paper and CAIS blog cite 4,157, and later versions and the GitHub README cite 3,668. The WMDP-Bio, WMDP-Chem and WMDP-Cyber labels are the three subsets.
about.what_it_tests: WMDP is a set of multiple-choice questions that serve as a proxy for hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity and chemical security. The questions were filtered by experts to remove sensitive and export-controlled details. Models are scored by accuracy, and the same questions are used in unlearning research, where the aim is to lower accuracy on the hazard questions while keeping general ability.

about.notes: Paper arXiv 2502.12404 (February 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: WMT24++ extends the WMT24 translation test set from English into 55 languages and dialects with human-written references. Translation quality is scored by an automatic metric; the Qwen cards use XCOMET-XXL and print an average over the 55 languages on a harder, rebalanced subset.

about.notes: The only candidate is an individual's Substack post found by search. It is not confirmed to be the benchmark Alibaba printed; the Qwen3.8 page lists WorkSpaceBench only as a row in its General Agent results table. The family may need to be dropped or re-scoped. Both WebFetch and the workstation browser were blocked on the post.
about.what_it_tests: WorkspaceBench is described in one post as a benchmark for agents working in OpenBB Workspace, where the durable state of the workspace is graded, for example whether a widget is in the correct dashboard and tab. The post could not be opened in this run because the site's bot check blocked the fetch, so the task count, inputs and scoring are not known. The Alibaba table row that prints the name has no description, method or citation.

about.notes: The GitHub README gives the 3,500 pairs, nine categories and judge model; the arXiv abstract (arXiv 2602.02537, submitted 28 January 2026, lead author Runjie Zhou, 19 authors) gives the title and purpose. Neither primary page describes a ForceAnswer setting, so the model-card label WorldVQA ForceAnswer is unverified and may be a different variant. Secondary leaderboards disagree on the leader and on scores, so no score is published here.
about.what_it_tests: WorldVQA tests atomic, vision-centric world knowledge in multimodal large language models: whether a model can recognise and name what is shown in an image, with recall separated from reasoning. The dataset has 3,500 VQA pairs across 9 categories, from common head-class objects to long-tail rarities. A judge model (an open-weights OpenAI model by default) grades the answers, and the leaderboard reports the first eight categories because the People category is excluded. The page refers to a 50% accuracy threshold and does not name the metric explicitly.

about.notes: The only description is the footnote on the Grok 4.1 Fast page: "X Browse is an internal benchmark that evaluates an agent's multihop search and browsing capabilities on X."
about.what_it_tests: X Browse is an internal xAI benchmark that tests an agent's multi-hop search and browsing on X (the social network): the agent has to find and combine posts to answer a question. Its questions and scoring are not published.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. FORTRESS is a Scale AI benchmark (Knight, Deshpande et al., 2025, arXiv 2506.14922, cited in the card's reference list); the FORTRESS-RN variant is named in the card and its link to the public suite is not further documented there. The card gives no release year, so introduced is null. The printed label reads CBRN / weapons refusals, which matches the card heading.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 9.3, CBRN / weapons refusals) reports how often the model refuses requests about chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons. The bio and chem parts use xAI's internal Autointent-Bio and Autointent-Chem suites of dangerous and benign CBRN queries, and the radiological and nuclear part uses FORTRESS-RN, a variant of the FORTRESS family of safeguard tests. The results are reported as refusal recall and refusal accuracy figures, and the card does not state the number of queries.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card gives no release year, so introduced is null. Test content is described only at the level the card gives.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 9.2, Child safety) describes an internal multi-turn evaluation of whether the model withholds assistance on child sexual exploitation, including CSAM. The prompts sit in the highest-severity child-safety category and unfold over a scripted conversation rather than a single message. A grader model judges each response against policy, and the reported figure is compliance, the share of dialogues that fail that judgment, where lower is better. The card does not state the number of dialogues.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card does not state the number of items or a release year, so those are null or omitted.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 9.1, General refusals) describes an internal evaluation of policy-following on harmful requests. The prompts span the major disallowed categories, from overt asks to well-hidden intent, and are written in English, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, Arabic and Russian. A grader model judges each response against policy, and the reported figure is compliance, the share of items that fail that judgment, where lower is better.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card names StrongREJECT but gives no reference for it, so that suite's authors are not stated here. The card does not state a release year or the number of attacks.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 8.1, Jailbreaks) reports how often the model complies with attacks that should be refused. It has three parts: a battery of standard jailbreaks, both published and internally discovered; StrongReject, the StrongREJECT suite; and long-horizon multi-turn jailbreaks, including Crescendo attacks. Each part is reported as compliance, the share of should-refuse attacks answered with disallowed help, and lower is better.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card gives no release year or prompt count.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 10.1, Self-harm refusals, in its mental-health part) checks whether the model declines to help with requests related to self-harm, including longer conversations, while still offering support and resources. A response also fails if the model refuses without redirecting the user to help, or cannot recognise the intent behind a message that implies self-harm or crisis. The reported figure is compliance, where a lower score is better, and the card does not describe the prompts.

about.notes: Written from xAI's own Grok 4.7 model card, read with pdftotext. The card gives no release year or item count. The card files it under its Behaviors part, section 11.
about.what_it_tests: xAI's Grok 4.7 model card (section 11.2, Sycophancy) describes an internal evaluation of whether the model abandons a correct answer when a user confidently states a wrong one. The items are factual questions in science, history and other general-knowledge topics, each paired with misleading user-supplied context. A grader compares the answer with the true answer, and the sycophancy rate is the share of items where the model follows the user instead of the correct answer, where lower is better.

about.maintainer: Bill Yuchen Lin and co-authors (Allen Institute for AI and University of Washington)
about.notes: Blog post 2024, paper arXiv 2502.01100 (February 2025). Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: ZebraLogic tests logical reasoning with 1,000 grid-based logic puzzles (zebra puzzles) of controlled size: the model has to assign attributes to houses so that every clue holds. The score is puzzle-level accuracy, which falls steeply as the grid grows.

about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 13 February 2025, revised 7 July 2026; ICML 2026) gives the purpose, the metrics and the release and one-year results. The question counts and the Cambridge affiliation come from the paper body as reported in secondary coverage, not from the abstract. "ZeroBench-main" on a model card is the 100 main questions.
about.what_it_tests: ZeroBench tests visual reasoning in multimodal models with questions filtered to be impossible for frontier models when it was built: 100 curated main questions plus 334 subquestions that break them into steps. The metrics are pass@1, pass^5 (all five attempts correct) and pass@5 (any of five attempts correct). At release every tested model scored 0% on pass@1 and pass^5; a year later the state of the art reached 6% pass^5 and 19% pass@5.

taxonomy_note: Sugra editorial taxonomy for navigating the collected catalog. It is not an international standard and not a claim that the whole industry has exactly 20 directions. One primary direction per family; overlaps are expressed by tags. A family is not a unit for comparing results: compare a specific test version and a compatible protocol.
